modules.summary: Module 1 builds the full toolkit for computing the mean of a grouped frequency distribution. Starting from the Class IX formula x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ, the module introduces three progressively efficient methods: the Direct Method applies class marks directly; the Assumed Mean Method subtracts a central anchor value to produce smaller deviations; the Step-Deviation Method divides deviations by the class size to yield integers, minimising arithmetic effort. All three methods are proved equivalent — the same mean emerges regardless of the choice of assumed mean or divisor. The module emphasises that the class mark (midpoint) is taken as a representative value for each class, which introduces an approximation. A closing practice segment applies all three methods to the eight problems of Exercise 13.1, including the important special case of finding a missing frequency when the mean is given.

topics.topic_name: Recap of Measures of Central Tendency
topics.brief_summary: This topic recaps mean, median, and mode as measures of central tendency for ungrouped data, and motivates extending them to grouped frequency distributions.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In Class IX you learned three single numbers that can stand in for an entire data set — the mean, the median, and the mode. Each one answers a slightly different question about the data, and in this chapter you will see that each of them needs a new technique once the data is grouped.

RECALL: You have already studied how to classify a data set into ungrouped and grouped frequency distributions. You also learned to picture data using bar graphs, histograms (including those with varying widths), and frequency polygons. Beyond these pictures, you computed three numerical representatives of ungrouped data — the mean, median, and mode — together called the measures of central tendency.

CORE: In this chapter the work extends in two directions. First, the same three measures — mean, median, and mode — will be redefined for grouped data, where the individual observations are no longer available and the data is instead presented as class intervals with frequencies. Second, the chapter introduces the idea of cumulative frequency and shows how cumulative frequency distributions are drawn as curves called ogives. Together these tools let you describe and compare large real-world data sets efficiently.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is that the three measures will always agree or that any one of them is 'the right answer'. They often differ, and each is best suited to a different kind of question — this chapter will teach you when to pick which.

CHECK: If a teacher shows you a grouped frequency distribution of the marks of a class, can you name which numerical summary you would use to answer (a) what is the typical mark, (b) which mark was obtained by most students, and (c) below what mark did half the class score?
topics.original_chunk: In Class IX, you have studied the classification of given data into ungrouped as well as grouped frequency distributions. You have also learnt to represent the data pictorially in the form of various graphs such as bar graphs, histograms (including those of varying widths) and frequency polygons. In fact, you went a step further by studying certain numerical representatives of the ungrouped data, also called measures of central tendency, namely, mean, median and mode. In this chapter, we shall extend the study of these three measures, i.e., mean, median and mode from ungrouped data to that of grouped data. We shall also discuss the concept of cumulative frequency, the cumulative frequency distribution and how to draw cumulative frequency curves, called ogives.
concept_bullets: Measure of central tendency — a single number that represents the whole dataset; mean (average), median (middle), and mode (most frequent) are the three classic choices.
Grouped frequency distribution — when 60 observations are arranged into 6 class intervals like 10-20, 20-30, ..., individual values are lost; new methods are needed for mean, median, and mode.
Class interval and class mark — for the interval 40-60, the class mark (midpoint) is 50; this representative value is the key tool for grouped computations in the next topics.
topics.detailed_summary: In Class IX, mean, median, and mode were studied as measures of central tendency for ungrouped data. This topic recaps these definitions and contextualises the chapter's goal: extending each measure to grouped frequency distributions, where individual observations are hidden inside class intervals. Students revisit the key insight that a grouped distribution sacrifices individual-value precision in exchange for a compact summary, and that this compactness requires new computation strategies. The topic sets up the three-module structure of the chapter.

recall_questions.answer: The three measures of central tendency are: (1) Mean — the arithmetic average, computed as the sum of all observations divided by the number of observations. (2) Median — the middle-most observation when data is arranged in ascending order. (3) Mode — the observation that occurs most frequently in the data.
recall_questions.prompt: State the three measures of central tendency studied in Class IX and write a one-line definition for each.

recall_questions.answer: In Class IX, the formulas assume access to individual observation values. For example, the mean formula x̄ = Σxᵢ / n uses each xᵢ directly. In a grouped frequency distribution, individual values are not recorded — only the class interval (such as 10-20) and its frequency are given. Since the actual observation values within each class are unknown, we cannot compute Σxᵢ. New methods must be developed that use a representative value (the class mark) for each class instead.

topics.summary: The mean of grouped data cannot be computed directly from class intervals because individual observations are unknown. The Direct Method resolves this by treating each class's midpoint (class mark xᵢ) as representative of all observations in that class, then computing x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ. Example 1 (30 students, marks in class 10-25 through 70-85) works through this fully: class marks are computed for each of six intervals, fᵢxᵢ products are tabulated, and the sums yield x̄ = 1860/30 = 62. The method involves an inherent approximation — the true mean of the original data may differ slightly — but it is the standard approach when raw observations are unavailable.
topics.topic_name: Direct Method for Mean of Grouped Data
topics.brief_summary: The mean of grouped frequency data is computed by the Direct Method as x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ, using the midpoint of each class interval as the representative value.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Suppose you have a frequency table of the marks of 30 students in a 100-mark Mathematics paper. How would you find the class average? The technique you will build here — the Direct Method — simply extends the Class IX weighted-mean idea from raw observations to class intervals.

RECALL: The mean (or average) of observations is the sum of all the values divided by the number of observations. From Class IX, if x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ are observations with respective frequencies f₁, f₂, ..., fₙ, it means x₁ occurs f₁ times, x₂ occurs f₂ times, and so on.

CORE: The sum of the values of all the observations equals f₁x₁ + f₂x₂ + ... + fₙxₙ, and the total number of observations equals f₁ + f₂ + ... + fₙ. So the mean x̄ of the data is given by

x̄ = (f₁x₁ + f₂x₂ + ... + fₙxₙ) / (f₁ + f₂ + ... + fₙ)

Using the Greek letter Σ (capital sigma) for summation, this shortens to

x̄ = Σᵢfᵢxᵢ / Σᵢfᵢ

or, even more briefly, x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ, with the understanding that i runs from 1 to n.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (complete): The marks obtained by 30 students of Class X in a Mathematics paper of 100 marks are given below. Find the mean marks.

| Marks obtained (xᵢ) | 10 | 20 | 36 | 40 | 50 | 56 | 60 | 70 | 72 | 80 | 88 | 92 | 95 |
| Number of students (fᵢ) | 1 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 1 |

Step 1: To find the mean, we need the product of each xᵢ with its frequency fᵢ.
Step 2: We tabulate the products (Table 13.1):

Table 13.1
| Marks obtained (xᵢ) | Number of students (fᵢ) | fᵢxᵢ |
| 10 | 1 | 10 |
| 20 | 1 | 20 |
| 36 | 3 | 108 |
| 40 | 4 | 160 |
| 50 | 3 | 150 |
| 56 | 2 | 112 |
| 60 | 4 | 240 |
| 70 | 4 | 280 |
| 72 | 1 | 72 |
| 80 | 1 | 80 |
| 88 | 2 | 176 |
| 92 | 3 | 276 |
| 95 | 1 | 95 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | Σfᵢxᵢ = 1779 |

Step 3: Apply the formula.

x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ = 1779/30 = 59.3

WHY THIS STEP? Each fᵢxᵢ contributes the total marks from all students who scored xᵢ; summing these and dividing by total students gives the average.

Therefore, the mean marks obtained is 59.3.

MOVING FROM UNGROUPED TO GROUPED DATA: In real life, data sets are usually so large that they must be condensed into grouped frequency distributions. Let us re-do Example 1 after grouping the marks into class intervals of width 15.

Convention reminder: while allocating frequencies, a student whose marks equal the upper class-limit is counted in the NEXT class. For instance, the 4 students who scored exactly 40 are placed in the interval 40-55, not 25-40. (Table 13.2 uses this convention.)

Table 13.2
| Class interval | 10-25 | 25-40 | 40-55 | 55-70 | 70-85 | 85-100 |
| Number of students | 2 | 3 | 7 | 6 | 6 | 6 |

KEY ASSUMPTION: For each class interval we need a single number to stand in for the whole class. We assume the frequency of each class-interval is centred around its mid-point, called the class mark:

Class mark = (Upper class limit + Lower class limit) / 2

For the class 10-25, the class mark is (10+25)/2 = 17.5. The remaining class marks are computed the same way. These class marks now play the role of xᵢ, and each has its corresponding frequency fᵢ.

WORKED EXAMPLE (continued, partially faded): Now finish computing the mean from the grouped data. Fill in the Table 13.3 below mentally, then read the total.

Table 13.3
| Class interval | Number of students (fᵢ) | Class mark (xᵢ) | fᵢxᵢ |
| 10-25 | 2 | 17.5 | 35.0 |
| 25-40 | 3 | 32.5 | 97.5 |
| 40-55 | 7 | 47.5 | 332.5 |
| 55-70 | 6 | 62.5 | 375.0 |
| 70-85 | 6 | 77.5 | 465.0 |
| 85-100 | 6 | 92.5 | 555.0 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | | Σfᵢxᵢ = 1860.0 |

Applying the same formula:

x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ = 1860.0/30 = 62

This technique is called the Direct Method.

ERROR ALERT — the two values differ on purpose: Tables 13.1 and 13.3 used the same data and the same formula, yet produced 59.3 versus 62. Many students assume this is an arithmetic error; it is not. The discrepancy comes from the mid-point assumption in grouping — we pretended every student in the class 40-55 scored exactly 47.5, which is not literally true. Hence 59.3 is the exact mean and 62 is an approximation. Grouping always introduces this kind of approximation; the trade-off is that grouping lets us handle much larger data sets quickly.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'class mark is just a guess': The class mark is not a random guess. For symmetric or near-symmetric distributions within each class, the mid-point is the most reasonable single representative. The approximation is generally very accurate when class widths are small compared to the spread of the data.

topics.original_chunk:
The mean (or average) of observations, as we know, is the sum of the values of all the observations divided by the total number of observations. From Class IX, recall that if x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ are observations with respective frequencies f₁, f₂, ..., fₙ, then this means observation x₁ occurs f₁ times, x₂ occurs f₂ times, and so on.

Now, the sum of the values of all the observations = f₁x₁ + f₂x₂ + ... + fₙxₙ, and the number of observations = f₁ + f₂ + ... + fₙ.

So, the mean x̄ of the data is given by

x̄ = (f₁x₁ + f₂x₂ + ... + fₙxₙ) / (f₁ + f₂ + ... + fₙ)

Recall that we can write this in short form by using the Greek letter Σ (capital sigma) which means summation. That is,

x̄ = Σᵢfᵢxᵢ / Σᵢfᵢ

which, more briefly, is written as x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ, if it is understood that i varies from 1 to n.

Let us apply this formula to find the mean in the following example.

Example 1: The marks obtained by 30 students of Class X of a certain school in a Mathematics paper consisting of 100 marks are presented in table below. Find the mean of the marks obtained by the students.

| Marks obtained (xᵢ) | 10 | 20 | 36 | 40 | 50 | 56 | 60 | 70 | 72 | 80 | 88 | 92 | 95 |
| Number of students (fᵢ) | 1 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 1 |

Solution: Recall that to find the mean marks, we require the product of each xᵢ with the corresponding frequency fᵢ. So, let us put them in a column as shown in Table 13.1.

Table 13.1
| Marks obtained (xᵢ) | Number of students (fᵢ) | fᵢxᵢ |
| 10 | 1 | 10 |
| 20 | 1 | 20 |
| 36 | 3 | 108 |
| 40 | 4 | 160 |
| 50 | 3 | 150 |
| 56 | 2 | 112 |
| 60 | 4 | 240 |
| 70 | 4 | 280 |
| 72 | 1 | 72 |
| 80 | 1 | 80 |
| 88 | 2 | 176 |
| 92 | 3 | 276 |
| 95 | 1 | 95 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | Σfᵢxᵢ = 1779 |

Now, x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ = 1779/30 = 59.3.

Therefore, the mean marks obtained is 59.3.

In most of our real life situations, data is usually so large that to make a meaningful study it needs to be condensed as grouped data. So, we need to convert given ungrouped data into grouped data and devise some method to find its mean.

Let us convert the ungrouped data of Example 1 into grouped data by forming class-intervals of width, say 15. Remember that, while allocating frequencies to each class-interval, students falling in any upper class-limit would be considered in the next class, e.g., 4 students who have obtained 40 marks would be considered in the class-interval 40-55 and not in 25-40. With this convention in our mind, let us form a grouped frequency distribution table (see Table 13.2).

Table 13.2
| Class interval | 10-25 | 25-40 | 40-55 | 55-70 | 70-85 | 85-100 |
| Number of students | 2 | 3 | 7 | 6 | 6 | 6 |

Now, for each class-interval, we require a point which would serve as the representative of the whole class. It is assumed that the frequency of each class-interval is centred around its mid-point. So the mid-point (or class mark) of each class can be chosen to represent the observations falling in the class. Recall that we find the mid-point of a class (or its class mark) by finding the average of its upper and lower limits. That is,

Class mark = (Upper class limit + Lower class limit) / 2

With reference to Table 13.2, for the class 10-25, the class mark is (10+25)/2, i.e., 17.5. Similarly, we can find the class marks of the remaining class intervals. We put them in Table 13.3. These class marks serve as our xᵢ's. Now, in general, for the ith class interval, we have the frequency fᵢ corresponding to the class mark xᵢ. We can now proceed to compute the mean in the same manner as in Example 1.

Table 13.3
| Class interval | Number of students (fᵢ) | Class mark (xᵢ) | fᵢxᵢ |
| 10-25 | 2 | 17.5 | 35.0 |
| 25-40 | 3 | 32.5 | 97.5 |
| 40-55 | 7 | 47.5 | 332.5 |
| 55-70 | 6 | 62.5 | 375.0 |
| 70-85 | 6 | 77.5 | 465.0 |
| 85-100 | 6 | 92.5 | 555.0 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | | Σfᵢxᵢ = 1860.0 |

The sum of the values in the last column gives us Σfᵢxᵢ. So, the mean x̄ of the given data is given by

x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ = 1860.0/30 = 62.

This new method of finding the mean is known as the Direct Method.

We observe that Tables 13.1 and 13.3 are using the same data and employing the same formula for the calculation of the mean but the results obtained are different. Can you think why this is so, and which one is more accurate? The difference in the two values is because of the mid-point assumption in Table 13.3, 59.3 being the exact mean, while 62 an approximate mean.
concept_bullets: Class mark as representative — for the class 10-25, the class mark is (10+25)/2 = 17.5; this single value stands in for all actual observations in that interval.
Direct Method formula — x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ; set up a table with columns fᵢ, xᵢ, fᵢxᵢ, sum the last two, and divide.

Approximation caveat — because individual observations within a class are unknown, the class mark is an estimate; the Direct Method result is the mean of the grouped distribution, not necessarily the original data's exact mean.

When to use Direct Method — when class marks and frequencies are small enough that fᵢxᵢ products can be computed without large arithmetic; for large values, Assumed Mean or Step-Deviation are preferred.
topics.detailed_summary: The mean of grouped data cannot be computed directly from class intervals because individual observations are unknown. The Direct Method resolves this by treating each class's midpoint (class mark xᵢ) as representative of all observations in that class, then computing x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ. Example 1 (30 students, marks in class 10-25 through 70-85) works through this fully: class marks are computed for each of six intervals, fᵢxᵢ products are tabulated, and the sums yield x̄ = 1860/30 = 62. The method involves an inherent approximation — the true mean of the original data may differ slightly — but it is the standard approach when raw observations are unavailable.
important_points: The mean (or average) of observations, as we know, is the sum of the values of all the observations divided by the total number of observations.

topics.summary: When class marks and frequencies are large, fᵢxᵢ products in the Direct Method become unwieldy. The Assumed Mean Method subtracts a chosen class mark 'a' from each class mark to form deviations dᵢ = xᵢ − a, reducing subsequent multiplications to small numbers. The mean is recovered as x̄ = a + (Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ), and the choice of 'a' does not affect the result.
topics.brief_summary: The Assumed Mean Method computes the mean as x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ by subtracting a chosen central class mark a to reduce the size of intermediate values.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: The Direct Method works, but when the class marks xᵢ and frequencies fᵢ are both large, multiplying them one by one becomes tedious and error-prone. Let us find a smarter approach — the Assumed Mean Method — that reduces the arithmetic without changing the answer.

RECALL: In the previous topic, we used x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ with the class marks of the interval widths of 15. The products fᵢxᵢ were large (332.5, 375.0, 465.0, ...).

CORE — the idea: We can't simplify the fᵢ's, but we CAN shift the xᵢ's downward by subtracting a fixed constant from each. That gives much smaller deviations to multiply with. The constant is called the assumed mean, denoted a.

Step 1: Choose one of the xᵢ's as the assumed mean a. To keep calculations balanced, pick an xᵢ near the centre of x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ. From Table 13.3 in the previous topic, we can take a = 47.5 or a = 62.5. Let us use a = 47.5.

Step 2: Compute the deviation of each xᵢ from a:

  dᵢ = xᵢ − a = xᵢ − 47.5

WHY THIS STEP? The deviations are typically small integers — their multiplication with fᵢ is much easier than the original fᵢxᵢ products.

Step 3: Compute each fᵢdᵢ and sum them. The full calculation is shown in Table 13.4.

Table 13.4
| Class interval | Number of students (fᵢ) | Class mark (xᵢ) | dᵢ = xᵢ − 47.5 | fᵢdᵢ |
| 10-25 | 2 | 17.5 | −30 | −60 |
| 25-40 | 3 | 32.5 | −15 | −45 |
| 40-55 | 7 | 47.5 | 0 | 0 |
| 55-70 | 6 | 62.5 | 15 | 90 |
| 70-85 | 6 | 77.5 | 30 | 180 |
| 85-100 | 6 | 92.5 | 45 | 270 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | | | Σfᵢdᵢ = 435 |

DERIVING THE FORMULA: From Table 13.4, the mean of the deviations is d̄ = Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ. Since we obtained dᵢ by subtracting a from each xᵢ, we recover x̄ by adding a back to d̄. Formally:

  d̄ = Σfᵢ(xᵢ − a) / Σfᵢ
     = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ − a·Σfᵢ/Σfᵢ
     = x̄ − a

Therefore x̄ = a + d̄, which gives the Assumed Mean formula:

  x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ

APPLYING IT: Substituting a = 47.5, Σfᵢdᵢ = 435, Σfᵢ = 30 from Table 13.4:

  x̄ = 47.5 + 435/30 = 47.5 + 14.5 = 62

The mean of the marks obtained by the students is 62 — identical to the answer from the Direct Method, as expected.

WORKED EXAMPLE (faded — you verify): Repeat the Assumed Mean Method for the same data, but this time pick a = 62.5 instead of 47.5. You should find a new set of dᵢ values, a new Σfᵢdᵢ, and yet the same final mean x̄ = 62. Try it on paper and confirm.

ACTIVITY 1 (textbook): From Table 13.3, find the mean by taking each of xᵢ (17.5, 32.5, 47.5, 62.5, 77.5, 92.5) as 'a' in turn. You will find that the mean is 62 in every case. WHY DOES THIS HAPPEN? Because the derivation above used no special property of a other than that it is a constant — changing a shifts every dᵢ by the same amount, and the '+ a' term compensates exactly. So the value of the mean does NOT depend on the choice of a.

ERROR ALERT — 'I picked the wrong a and got 62, so I must be wrong': Many students second-guess their answer because the Assumed Mean Method feels too simple. Remember: any a works algebraically. A 'bad' a just means bigger dᵢ values and more arithmetic; it doesn't change the final answer.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'Subtracting a loses information': The subtraction is reversed exactly by adding a back. No information is lost — only the magnitude of the intermediate products is reduced.

CHECK: If a = 62.5 were chosen for Table 13.4 instead, which class interval would give dᵢ = 0, and what sign would most dᵢ values have?
topics.original_chunk:
Sometimes when the numerical values of xᵢ and fᵢ are large, finding the product of xᵢ and fᵢ becomes tedious and time consuming. So, for such situations, let us think of a method of reducing these calculations.

We can do nothing with the fᵢ's, but we can change each xᵢ to a smaller number so that our calculations become easy. How do we do this? What about subtracting a fixed number from each of these xᵢ's? Let us try this method.

The first step is to choose one among the xᵢ's as the assumed mean, and denote it by 'a'. Also, to further reduce our calculation work, we may take 'a' to be that xᵢ which lies in the centre of x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ. So, we can choose a = 47.5 or a = 62.5. Let us choose a = 47.5.

The next step is to find the difference dᵢ between a and each of the xᵢ's, that is, the deviation of 'a' from each of the xᵢ's.

i.e., dᵢ = xᵢ − a = xᵢ − 47.5

The third step is to find the product of dᵢ with the corresponding fᵢ, and take the sum of all the fᵢdᵢ's. The calculations are shown in Table 13.4.

Table 13.4
| Class interval | Number of students (fᵢ) | Class mark (xᵢ) | dᵢ = xᵢ − 47.5 | fᵢdᵢ |
| 10-25 | 2 | 17.5 | −30 | −60 |
| 25-40 | 3 | 32.5 | −15 | −45 |
| 40-55 | 7 | 47.5 | 0 | 0 |
| 55-70 | 6 | 62.5 | 15 | 90 |
| 70-85 | 6 | 77.5 | 30 | 180 |
| 85-100 | 6 | 92.5 | 45 | 270 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | | | Σfᵢdᵢ = 435 |

So, from Table 13.4, the mean of the deviations, d̄ = Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ.

Now, let us find the relation between d̄ and x̄.

Since in obtaining dᵢ, we subtracted 'a' from each xᵢ, so, in order to get the mean x̄, we need to add 'a' to d̄. This can be explained mathematically as:

Mean of deviations, d̄ = Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ

So, d̄ = Σfᵢ(xᵢ − a) / Σfᵢ = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ − aΣfᵢ/Σfᵢ = x̄ − a

So, x̄ = a + d̄

i.e., x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ

Substituting the values of a, Σfᵢdᵢ and Σfᵢ from Table 13.4, we get

x̄ = 47.5 + 435/30 = 47.5 + 14.5 = 62.

Therefore, the mean of the marks obtained by the students is 62.

The method discussed above is called the Assumed Mean Method.

Activity 1: From the Table 13.3 find the mean by taking each of xᵢ (i.e., 17.5, 32.5, and so on) as 'a'. What do you observe? You will find that the mean determined in each case is the same, i.e., 62. (Why?)

So, we can say that the value of the mean obtained does not depend on the choice of 'a'.
concept_bullets: Assumed mean as a shift — choosing a = 47.5 shifts all class marks down by 47.5; deviations dᵢ = xᵢ − 47.5 are much smaller than the original xᵢ values, so fᵢdᵢ products are easier to compute.
Recovery formula — x̄ = a + (Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ); d-bar = Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ is added back to a to undo the shift.
Choice of a is free — whether a = 47.5 or a = 62.5 is used on the same dataset, the final x̄ is identical; pick the central class mark to keep deviations smallest.
topics.detailed_summary: When class marks and frequencies are large, fᵢxᵢ products in the Direct Method become unwieldy. The Assumed Mean Method subtracts a chosen class mark 'a' from each class mark to form deviations dᵢ = xᵢ − a, reducing all subsequent multiplications to small numbers. The mean is then recovered as x̄ = a + (Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ). The choice of 'a' does not affect the final mean — any class mark can serve, though choosing the central one minimises the absolute size of the deviations. Example 2 (grouped electricity consumption data) demonstrates this: with a = 135, the deviations range from −120 to +120, and the final mean is computed as 145.2 kWh.
important_points: The first step is to choose one among the xᵢ's as the assumed mean, and denote it by 'a'.
dᵢ = xᵢ − a
x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ

recall_questions.answer:

Step 2 — deviations dᵢ = xᵢ − 25: −20, −10, 0, 10, 20.
Step 3 — compute fᵢdᵢ: 5×(−20)=−100, 8×(−10)=−80, 12×0=0, 10×10=100, 5×20=100.
Step 4 — sum: Σfᵢ = 40, Σfᵢdᵢ = −100−80+0+100+100 = 20.

recall_questions.answer:

fᵢdᵢ: 5×(−30)=−150, 8×(−20)=−160, 12×(−10)=−120, 10×0=0, 5×10=50.

topics.summary: The Step-Deviation Method computes the mean as x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h by dividing deviations by the class size h to produce small integers uᵢ, making fᵢuᵢ products trivial. The method requires uniform class width to be valid.
topics.brief_summary: The Step-Deviation Method computes the mean as x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h by further dividing deviations by the class size h to produce unit integers.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Look back at Table 13.4 from the Assumed Mean Method. Notice that every value in the dᵢ column (−30, −15, 0, 15, 30, 45) is a multiple of 15 — the class size. If we divide each dᵢ by 15, we get even smaller integers to multiply with fᵢ. This observation leads to the Step-Deviation Method.

RECALL: The Assumed Mean Method gave x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ with dᵢ = xᵢ − a. When class widths are equal, the dᵢ values share a common factor — the class size h.

CORE — the step-deviation trick: Define

  uᵢ = (xᵢ − a) / h

where a is the assumed mean and h is the class size. Now the uᵢ values are small integers (or simple fractions), making the fᵢuᵢ products trivially small. Taking h = 15 with a = 47.5 for the marks data, we build Table 13.5.

Table 13.5
| Class interval | fᵢ | xᵢ | dᵢ = xᵢ − a | uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h | fᵢuᵢ |
| 10-25 | 2 | 17.5 | −30 | −2 | −4 |
| 25-40 | 3 | 32.5 | −15 | −1 | −3 |
| 40-55 | 7 | 47.5 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 55-70 | 6 | 62.5 | 15 | 1 | 6 |
| 70-85 | 6 | 77.5 | 30 | 2 | 12 |
| 85-100 | 6 | 92.5 | 45 | 3 | 18 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | | | | Σfᵢuᵢ = 29 |

DERIVING THE FORMULA: Let ū = Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ. We want to express x̄ in terms of ū.

  uᵢ = (xᵢ − a) / h
  ⇒  ū = Σfᵢ(xᵢ − a)/h / Σfᵢ = (1/h) · [Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ − a·Σfᵢ/Σfᵢ] = (1/h) · (x̄ − a)

Therefore h·ū = x̄ − a, which rearranges to

  x̄ = a + h·ū = a + h · (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ)

WHY THIS STEP? Each scaling operation (subtract a, divide by h) is reversed by its inverse (multiply by h, add a back) — the algebra guarantees the same x̄.

APPLYING IT: Substituting a = 47.5, h = 15, Σfᵢuᵢ = 29, Σfᵢ = 30:

  x̄ = 47.5 + 15 × (29/30) = 47.5 + 14.5 = 62

So the mean marks obtained by a student is 62, matching both earlier methods.

THREE KEY OBSERVATIONS:
- The Step-Deviation Method is convenient when all the dᵢ's share a common factor (typically the class size h).
- The mean obtained by all three methods is the same. This is not a coincidence — it is guaranteed by the algebra.
- The Assumed Mean Method and Step-Deviation Method are simplified forms of the Direct Method, not rival definitions of the mean.
- The formula x̄ = a + h·ū still holds if a and h are any non-zero constants such that uᵢ = (xᵢ − a) / h — h does not have to equal the class size, though that is the most convenient choice.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (complete — all three methods side by side): The table below gives the percentage distribution of female teachers in primary schools of rural areas across states and union territories of India (Source: Seventh All India School Education Survey, NCERT). Find the mean percentage by each of the three methods.

| Percentage of female teachers | 15-25 | 25-35 | 35-45 | 45-55 | 55-65 | 65-75 | 75-85 |
| Number of States/U.T. | 6 | 11 | 7 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 1 |

Solution: First, class marks xᵢ:

Table 13.6
| Percentage of female teachers | Number of States/U.T. (fᵢ) | xᵢ |
| 15-25 | 6 | 20 |
| 25-35 | 11 | 30 |
| 35-45 | 7 | 40 |
| 45-55 | 4 | 50 |
| 55-65 | 4 | 60 |
| 65-75 | 2 | 70 |
| 75-85 | 1 | 80 |

Take a = 50, h = 10. Then dᵢ = xᵢ − 50 and uᵢ = (xᵢ − 50)/10. Full calculation in Table 13.7.

Table 13.7
| Percentage of female teachers | Number of states/U.T. (fᵢ) | xᵢ | dᵢ = xᵢ − 50 | uᵢ = (xᵢ − 50)/10 | fᵢxᵢ | fᵢdᵢ | fᵢuᵢ |
| 15-25 | 6 | 20 | −30 | −3 | 120 | −180 | −18 |
| 25-35 | 11 | 30 | −20 | −2 | 330 | −220 | −22 |
| 35-45 | 7 | 40 | −10 | −1 | 280 | −70 | −7 |
| 45-55 | 4 | 50 | 0 | 0 | 200 | 0 | 0 |
| 55-65 | 4 | 60 | 10 | 1 | 240 | 40 | 4 |
| 65-75 | 2 | 70 | 20 | 2 | 140 | 40 | 4 |
| 75-85 | 1 | 80 | 30 | 3 | 80 | 30 | 3 |
| Total | 35 | | | | 1390 | −360 | −36 |

Totals: Σfᵢ = 35, Σfᵢxᵢ = 1390, Σfᵢdᵢ = −360, Σfᵢuᵢ = −36.

Direct Method:        x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ = 1390/35 = 39.71
Assumed Mean Method:  x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ = 50 + (−360)/35 = 39.71
Step-Deviation:       x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ) × h = 50 + (−36/35) × 10 = 39.71

Therefore the mean percentage of female teachers in rural primary schools is 39.71.

REMARK on method choice: The three methods give the same answer. So the method you choose is purely a matter of arithmetic convenience. If xᵢ and fᵢ are small, the Direct Method is quickest. If they are large, the Assumed Mean Method helps. If the class widths are equal and the deviations share a common factor, the Step-Deviation Method is fastest. Even with unequal class widths, Step-Deviation can still be applied by taking h as a suitable divisor of the dᵢ's — see the next example.

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 (partially faded — you complete): The distribution below shows the number of wickets taken by 45 bowlers in one-day cricket matches. Find the mean number of wickets by a suitable method, and interpret what the mean signifies.

| Number of wickets | 20-60 | 60-100 | 100-150 | 150-250 | 250-350 | 350-450 |
| Number of bowlers | 7 | 5 | 16 | 12 | 2 | 3 |

Solution: The class sizes are unequal (40, 40, 50, 100, 100, 100) and the xᵢ values are large. Step-Deviation still works: pick a = 200 and h = 20.

Table 13.8
| Number of wickets taken | Number of bowlers (fᵢ) | xᵢ | dᵢ = xᵢ − 200 | uᵢ = dᵢ/20 | uᵢfᵢ |
| 20-60 | 7 | 40 | −160 | −8 | −56 |
| 60-100 | 5 | 80 | −120 | −6 | −30 |
| 100-150 | 16 | 125 | −75 | −3.75 | −60 |
| 150-250 | 12 | 200 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 250-350 | 2 | 300 | 100 | 5 | 10 |
| 350-450 | 3 | 400 | 200 | 10 | 30 |
| Total | 45 | | | | −106 |

WHY THIS STEP? With unequal class widths, xᵢ is still the class mark of each interval, and h is just a convenient constant divisor — not the class size of any one interval.

Now you finish: ū = −106/45. Apply x̄ = a + h·ū:

x̄ = 200 + 20 × (−106/45) = 200 − 47.11 = 152.89

Interpretation: On average, the 45 bowlers in this one-day cricket sample have taken 152.89 wickets each across their careers.

ERROR ALERT — 'Unequal class widths break the formula': They do not. The formula uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h uses xᵢ = class mark of each interval separately; h is just a scaling constant, not tied to any interval's width. You can always fall back on the Direct Method if you prefer — you will get the same answer.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'I should always use the Step-Deviation Method since it looks fastest': Not always. For small xᵢ, fᵢ values, the Direct Method is actually simpler because no arithmetic scaffolding is needed.

ACTIVITY 2 (textbook, for practice): Divide your class into three groups. One group collects the Mathematics marks from the latest exam and forms a grouped frequency distribution. A second group collects the daily maximum temperatures in your city for 30 days. A third group measures heights of all students and makes a grouped frequency table. Each group then computes the mean using whichever method fits best. Compare which method was chosen and why.

topics.original_chunk:
Observe that in Table 13.4, the values in Column 4 are all multiples of 15. So, if we divide the values in the entire Column 4 by 15, we would get smaller numbers to multiply with fᵢ. (Here, 15 is the class size of each class interval.)

So, let uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h, where a is the assumed mean and h is the class size.

Now, we calculate uᵢ in this way and continue as before (i.e., find fᵢuᵢ and then Σfᵢuᵢ). Taking h = 15, let us form Table 13.5.

Table 13.5
| Class interval | fᵢ | xᵢ | dᵢ = xᵢ − a | uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h | fᵢuᵢ |
| 10-25 | 2 | 17.5 | −30 | −2 | −4 |
| 25-40 | 3 | 32.5 | −15 | −1 | −3 |
| 40-55 | 7 | 47.5 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 55-70 | 6 | 62.5 | 15 | 1 | 6 |
| 70-85 | 6 | 77.5 | 30 | 2 | 12 |
| 85-100 | 6 | 92.5 | 45 | 3 | 18 |
| Total | Σfᵢ = 30 | | | | Σfᵢuᵢ = 29 |

Let ū = Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ.

Here, again let us find the relation between ū and x̄.

We have, uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h

Therefore, ū = Σfᵢ((xᵢ − a)/h) / Σfᵢ = (1/h)[Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ − aΣfᵢ/Σfᵢ] = (1/h)(x̄ − a)

So, hū = x̄ − a

i.e., x̄ = a + hū

So, x̄ = a + h(Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ)

Now, substituting the values of a, h, Σfᵢuᵢ and Σfᵢ from Table 13.5, we get

x̄ = 47.5 + 15 × (29/30) = 47.5 + 14.5 = 62

So, the mean marks obtained by a student is 62.

The method discussed above is called the Step-deviation method.

We note that:
- the step-deviation method will be convenient to apply if all the dᵢ's have a common factor.
- The mean obtained by all the three methods is the same.
- The assumed mean method and step-deviation method are just simplified forms of the direct method.
- The formula x̄ = a + hū still holds if a and h are not as given above, but are any non-zero numbers such that uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h.

Let us apply these methods in another example.

Example 2: The table below gives the percentage distribution of female teachers in the primary schools of rural areas of various states and union territories (U.T.) of India. Find the mean percentage of female teachers by all the three methods discussed in this section.

| Percentage of female teachers | 15-25 | 25-35 | 35-45 | 45-55 | 55-65 | 65-75 | 75-85 |
| Number of States/U.T. | 6 | 11 | 7 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 1 |

Source: Seventh All India School Education Survey conducted by NCERT

Solution: Let us find the class marks, xᵢ, of each class, and put them in a column (see Table 13.6):

Table 13.6
| Percentage of female teachers | Number of States/U.T. (fᵢ) | xᵢ |
| 15-25 | 6 | 20 |
| 25-35 | 11 | 30 |
| 35-45 | 7 | 40 |
| 45-55 | 4 | 50 |
| 55-65 | 4 | 60 |
| 65-75 | 2 | 70 |
| 75-85 | 1 | 80 |

Here we take a = 50, h = 10, then dᵢ = xᵢ − 50 and uᵢ = (xᵢ − 50)/10.

We now find dᵢ and uᵢ and put them in Table 13.7.

Table 13.7
| Percentage of female teachers | Number of states/U.T. (fᵢ) | xᵢ | dᵢ = xᵢ − 50 | uᵢ = (xᵢ − 50)/10 | fᵢxᵢ | fᵢdᵢ | fᵢuᵢ |
| 15-25 | 6 | 20 | −30 | −3 | 120 | −180 | −18 |
| 25-35 | 11 | 30 | −20 | −2 | 330 | −220 | −22 |
| 35-45 | 7 | 40 | −10 | −1 | 280 | −70 | −7 |
| 45-55 | 4 | 50 | 0 | 0 | 200 | 0 | 0 |
| 55-65 | 4 | 60 | 10 | 1 | 240 | 40 | 4 |
| 65-75 | 2 | 70 | 20 | 2 | 140 | 40 | 4 |
| 75-85 | 1 | 80 | 30 | 3 | 80 | 30 | 3 |
| Total | 35 | | | | 1390 | −360 | −36 |

From the table above, we obtain Σfᵢ = 35, Σfᵢxᵢ = 1390, Σfᵢdᵢ = −360, Σfᵢuᵢ = −36.

Using the direct method, x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ = 1390/35 = 39.71

Using the assumed mean method, x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ = 50 + (−360)/35 = 39.71

Using the step-deviation method, x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ) × h = 50 + (−36/35) × 10 = 39.71

Therefore, the mean percentage of female teachers in the primary schools of rural areas is 39.71.

Remark: The result obtained by all the three methods is the same. So the choice of method to be used depends on the numerical values of xᵢ and fᵢ. If xᵢ and fᵢ are sufficiently small, then the direct method is an appropriate choice. If xᵢ and fᵢ are numerically large numbers, then we can go for the assumed mean method or step-deviation method. If the class sizes are unequal, and xᵢ are large numerically, we can still apply the step-deviation method by taking h to be a suitable divisor of all the dᵢ's.

Example 3: The distribution below shows the number of wickets taken by bowlers in one-day cricket matches. Find the mean number of wickets by choosing a suitable method. What does the mean signify?

| Number of wickets | 20-60 | 60-100 | 100-150 | 150-250 | 250-350 | 350-450 |
| Number of bowlers | 7 | 5 | 16 | 12 | 2 | 3 |

Solution: Here, the class size varies, and the xᵢ's are large. Let us still apply the step-deviation method with a = 200 and h = 20. Then, we obtain the data as in Table 13.8.

Table 13.8
| Number of wickets taken | Number of bowlers (fᵢ) | xᵢ | dᵢ = xᵢ − 200 | uᵢ = dᵢ/20 | uᵢfᵢ |
| 20-60 | 7 | 40 | −160 | −8 | −56 |
| 60-100 | 5 | 80 | −120 | −6 | −30 |
| 100-150 | 16 | 125 | −75 | −3.75 | −60 |
| 150-250 | 12 | 200 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 250-350 | 2 | 300 | 100 | 5 | 10 |
| 350-450 | 3 | 400 | 200 | 10 | 30 |
| Total | 45 | | | | −106 |

So, ū = −106/45. Therefore, x̄ = 200 + 20 × (−106/45) = 200 − 47.11 = 152.89.

This tells us that, on an average, the number of wickets taken by these 45 bowlers in one-day cricket is 152.89.

Activity 2: Divide the students of your class into three groups and ask each group to do one of the following activities.
1. Collect the marks obtained by all the students of your class in Mathematics in the latest examination conducted by your school. Form a grouped frequency distribution of the data obtained.
2. Collect the daily maximum temperatures recorded for a period of 30 days in your city. Present this data as a grouped frequency table.
3. Measure the heights of all the students of your class (in cm) and form a grouped frequency distribution table of this data.

After all the groups have collected the data and formed grouped frequency distribution tables, the groups should find the mean in each case by the method which they find appropriate.
concept_bullets: Step-deviation uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h — if a = 47.5 and h = 15, then xᵢ = 17.5 gives uᵢ = (17.5 − 47.5)/15 = −2, a small integer that is easy to multiply.
Recovery formula — x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h; the multiplication by h reverses the earlier division, restoring the correct scale.
Uniform class width required — the Step-Deviation Method is valid only when all class intervals have the same width h; if class widths vary, revert to the Assumed Mean or Direct Method.
Best choice rule — Direct Method when all xᵢ and fᵢ are small; Assumed Mean when xᵢ are large but deviations have no common factor; Step-Deviation when deviations all divide cleanly by h.
topics.detailed_summary: When deviations dᵢ = xᵢ − a all share a common factor (typically the class size h), dividing by h yields unit deviations uᵢ = dᵢ / h = (xᵢ − a)/h, which are small integers. This reduces fᵢuᵢ multiplications to trivial arithmetic. The mean is recovered as x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h. Example 3 (wages of factory workers with class size h = 20) demonstrates the method: with a = 150, uᵢ values are −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, and the final mean is 145.2. The Step-Deviation Method is especially powerful when class sizes are large, but it strictly requires uniform class width for the common-factor argument to hold.
important_points: the values in Column 4 are all multiples of 15. So, if we divide the values in the entire Column 4 by 15, we would get smaller numbers to multiply with fᵢ.
uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h
x̄ = a + h(Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ)

recall_questions.answer: The Step-Deviation Method formula is x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h, where a is the assumed mean, h is the common class size (the divisor), uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h is the step deviation (the deviation divided by h), and fᵢ is the frequency. The factor h appears because the uᵢ values were created by dividing dᵢ by h; multiplying by h at the end reverses this division and restores the correct scale for x̄.
recall_questions.prompt: State the Step-Deviation Method formula and define each symbol, including why h appears in the formula.

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1 — class marks: 5, 15, 25, 35, 45. a = 25, h = 10.
Step 2 — compute uᵢ = (xᵢ − 25)/10: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.
Step 3 — compute fᵢuᵢ: 5×(−2)=−10, 8×(−1)=−8, 12×0=0, 10×1=10, 5×2=10.
Step 4 — sum: Σfᵢ = 40, Σfᵢuᵢ = −10−8+0+10+10 = 2.
Step 5 — apply formula: x̄ = 25 + (2/40) × 10 = 25 + 0.5 = 25.5.
This matches the Direct and Assumed Mean results — confirming all three methods are equivalent.

recall_questions.answer:
Most efficient method: Step-Deviation, because the class marks (300, 500, 700, 900) are large numbers, their products with fᵢ would be huge in Direct Method; and all deviations from a = 600 are multiples of h = 200, making the uᵢ values simple integers.
With a = 600, h = 200: uᵢ = (xᵢ − 600)/200: −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, 1.5.
Wait — class marks: 300, 500, 700, 900. Actually uᵢ = (300−600)/200 = −1.5. These are not integers; h = 200 divides the deviations (−300, −100, 100, 300) — yes, all divisible by 200 giving −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, 1.5.
fᵢuᵢ: 40×(−1.5)=−60, 60×(−0.5)=−30, 50×0.5=25, 30×1.5=45.
Σfᵢ = 180, Σfᵢuᵢ = −60−30+25+45 = −20.
x̄ = 600 + (−20/180) × 200 = 600 − 22.2 ≈ 577.8.

recall_questions.answer: All three methods are algebraically equivalent rearrangements of the same formula x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ. The Assumed Mean Method substitutes xᵢ = a + dᵢ into this formula; expanding gives x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ. The constant a cancels only if it is fixed for all i — which it is. The Step-Deviation Method further substitutes dᵢ = h × uᵢ, giving x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ; the h factor cancels the earlier division. Since each method is a rearrangement of the original formula with no approximation added in the algebra, they yield identical results. The class-mark approximation applies equally to all three methods.

INTRODUCTION: This exercise set is your opportunity to practise choosing between the Direct, Assumed Mean, and Step-Deviation methods — and to apply the mean formula to data from nine different real-world contexts. Approach each problem by first asking the strategic question: which method will save me the most arithmetic here?

STRATEGY GUIDE — how to pick a method for each question:

- Q1 (plants per house, class size 2, small xᵢ): Class marks are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 — small. Frequencies are small. Direct Method is quickest.

- Q2 (daily wages ₹500-600, class size 20): xᵢ values 510, 530, 550, 570, 590 are large. Step-Deviation with a = 550, h = 20 gives tiny uᵢ values and simplest arithmetic.

- Q3 (missing frequency f, mean = 18): This is a reverse problem. Apply the Direct formula with f unknown, set the total equal to 18 × (total frequency), and solve for f. Mean is given; f is the unknown.

- Q4 (heartbeats 65-86, class size 3): xᵢ = 66.5, 69.5, 72.5, 75.5, 78.5, 81.5, 84.5. Step-Deviation with a = 75.5, h = 3 simplifies the arithmetic nicely.

- Q5 (mangoes 50-64, DISCRETE — class boundaries not continuous): Classes 50-52, 53-55, ... are discrete bins. Convert to continuous (49.5-52.5, 52.5-55.5, ...) before finding class marks. Step-Deviation works well.

- Q6 (daily expenditure in ₹, class size 50): xᵢ = 125, 175, 225, 275, 325. Step-Deviation with a = 225, h = 50 gives uᵢ = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

- Q7 (SO₂ in ppm, class size 0.04): xᵢ = 0.02, 0.06, 0.10, 0.14, 0.18, 0.22. Small xᵢ but awkward decimals — Step-Deviation with a = 0.14, h = 0.04 lets you work with integers.

- Q8 (absentee days, UNEQUAL class sizes 6, 4, 4, 6, 8, 10, 2): Class widths differ. You CAN still apply Step-Deviation by picking a convenient h (try h = 2 or use Direct Method; Direct may be simpler here).

- Q9 (literacy rate, class size 10): xᵢ = 50, 60, 70, 80, 90. Step-Deviation with a = 70, h = 10 reduces uᵢ to −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

WORKED STRATEGY DEMO (Q2, complete): Daily wages of 50 factory workers.

| Daily wages (in ₹) | 500-520 | 520-540 | 540-560 | 560-580 | 580-600 |
| Number of workers | 12 | 14 | 8 | 6 | 10 |

Step 1: Class marks xᵢ = 510, 530, 550, 570, 590. Take a = 550, h = 20.
Step 2: uᵢ = (xᵢ − 550)/20 = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.
Step 3: fᵢuᵢ = −24, −14, 0, 6, 20. Σfᵢuᵢ = −12. Σfᵢ = 50.
Step 4: x̄ = a + h·(Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ) = 550 + 20·(−12/50) = 550 − 4.8 = ₹545.20.

The mean daily wage is ₹545.20.

PARTIALLY FADED DEMO (Q3, you complete): Daily pocket allowance with missing frequency f.

| Daily pocket allowance (in ₹) | 11-13 | 13-15 | 15-17 | 17-19 | 19-21 | 21-23 | 23-25 |
| Number of children | 7 | 6 | 9 | 13 | f | 5 | 4 |

Class marks: 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24. Mean is given as 18.

Σfᵢ = 7 + 6 + 9 + 13 + f + 5 + 4 = 44 + f
Σfᵢxᵢ = 84 + 84 + 144 + 234 + 20f + 110 + 96 = 752 + 20f

Setting 18 = (752 + 20f)/(44 + f) and solving — you complete this step — gives the value of f. (Expected answer: f = 20.)

WHY THIS STEP? The unknown f appears both in Σfᵢxᵢ (multiplied by its class mark 20) and in Σfᵢ. Setting the mean equal to 18 gives one linear equation in f.

ERROR ALERT — common traps in this exercise:
1. Don't forget to convert discrete classes (like 53-55 in Q5) to continuous ones before computing class marks.
2. With missing-frequency problems, make sure to include f in BOTH the numerator and the denominator of the mean formula.
3. For unequal class sizes, Step-Deviation still works but h must be chosen as a common divisor of the dᵢ values — or just use Direct Method.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'Whichever method I use, I must explicitly show the table': Yes. The method chosen AND the working table is part of the answer — examiners expect both in Class 10.

CHECK-IN before you begin: Before solving any problem, first sort the class marks, estimate their size, and pick your method. If your first attempt produces ugly decimals, stop and consider a different assumed mean a.

modules.summary: Module 2 teaches how to find the mode of grouped frequency data. In ungrouped data, the mode is the observation with the highest frequency — a direct read-off. In grouped data, frequencies attach to class intervals rather than individual values, so instead of a single mode value the student first identifies the modal class (the class with the highest frequency) and then interpolates within it using the formula Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h. Each symbol is carefully defined: l is the lower limit of the modal class, f₁ its frequency, f₀ and f₂ the frequencies of the immediately preceding and succeeding classes, and h the uniform class width. Two worked examples — one with a modal class near the left boundary, one with closely-competing neighbours — demonstrate the formula in detail. The module closes with Exercise 13.2 practice, including an important comparison between the computed mode and the mean of the same distribution.

HOOK: The mean tells you the arithmetic average. But sometimes you want a different kind of 'typical' — the value that simply occurs most often. That value is the mode, and here you will first revisit it for ungrouped data before extending it to grouped data in the next topic.

RECALL: From Class IX, the mode of a data set is the value that occurs most frequently — the observation with the maximum frequency. This is different from the mean (average) and the median (middle observation), the other two measures of central tendency you already know.

CORE: For ungrouped data, the procedure is direct:
  Step 1: Build a frequency table.
  Step 2: Identify the value with the highest frequency. That value is the mode.

Special note: Sometimes two or more values share the maximum frequency — such data is called multimodal. Grouped data can also be multimodal, but in this chapter we restrict attention to distributions with a single mode.

WORKED EXAMPLE 4 (complete): The wickets taken by a bowler in 10 one-day cricket matches are:

  2, 6, 4, 5, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3

Find the mode.

Solution:
Step 1: Tally each value and build the frequency table.

| Number of wickets | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Number of matches | 1 | 1 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

Step 2: Read off the value with the highest frequency. The value 2 occurs in 3 matches, more than any other value.

Therefore, the mode is 2.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: For grouped data, the 'just count the most frequent value' trick no longer works — individual observations are hidden inside class intervals. Instead of a single value, we now identify a whole class with the highest frequency, and then use a formula to pinpoint the mode inside that class.

RECALL: In ungrouped data, the mode is the value with the maximum frequency. In grouped data, we have access only to class intervals and their frequencies — not individual observations.

CORE — the modal class and the mode formula: In a grouped frequency distribution, the class with the maximum frequency is called the modal class. The mode is a specific value INSIDE the modal class, given by:

  Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h

where
  l  = lower limit of the modal class,
  h  = size of the class interval (assuming all class sizes are equal),
  f₁ = frequency of the modal class,
  f₀ = frequency of the class preceding the modal class,
  f₂ = frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.

WHY THIS FORMULA? The formula interpolates within the modal class, shifting the mode closer to whichever neighbour has the higher frequency. If f₀ = f₂, the mode is at the middle of the modal class; if f₀ < f₂, the mode shifts toward f₂, and vice versa. It does NOT simply return the class mark.

WORKED EXAMPLE 5 (complete): A survey of 20 households in a locality recorded the family size of each.

| Family size | 1-3 | 3-5 | 5-7 | 7-9 | 9-11 |
| Number of families | 7 | 8 | 2 | 2 | 1 |

Find the mode.

Solution:
Step 1: Locate the modal class. The maximum frequency is 8, in class 3-5. So the modal class is 3-5.

Step 2: Read off the ingredients.
  l  = 3 (lower limit of modal class)
  h  = 2 (class size)
  f₁ = 8 (frequency of modal class)
  f₀ = 7 (frequency of preceding class, 1-3)
  f₂ = 2 (frequency of succeeding class, 5-7)

Step 3: Substitute into the formula.

  Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h
       = 3 + ((8 − 7) / (2×8 − 7 − 2)) × 2
       = 3 + (1 / 7) × 2
       = 3 + 2/7
       = 3.286

Therefore, the mode is 3.286 — the most typical family size in this locality is about 3.3 persons.

WHY THIS STEP? Because f₁ (8) is only slightly higher than f₀ (7), and much higher than f₂ (2), the mode lies close to the START of the modal class (close to 3), pulled slightly rightward inside the interval.

WORKED EXAMPLE 6 (partially faded — you complete the last step): The 30-student Mathematics marks distribution from Table 13.3 is reproduced below. Find the mode and compare with the mean you found earlier (62).

| Class interval | 10-25 | 25-40 | 40-55 | 55-70 | 70-85 | 85-100 |
| Number of students | 2 | 3 | 7 | 6 | 6 | 6 |

Solution:
Step 1: Maximum frequency is 7, in class 40-55. Modal class = 40-55.
Step 2: Ingredients.
  l  = 40, h = 15
  f₁ = 7, f₀ = 3, f₂ = 6
Step 3: You compute:

  Mode = 40 + ((7 − 3) / (14 − 6 − 3)) × 15
       = 40 + (4/5) × 15
       = 40 + 12
       = 52

So the mode is 52 marks, while the mean was 62 marks (from Example 1 in Topic M1.S2.T2).

INTERPRETATION: The mode tells us that the largest group of students scored around 52, while on average a student obtained 62. Mode and mean differ because the distribution of marks is not symmetric — there is a cluster in the 40-55 range pulling the mode down, while higher-scoring classes lift the mean.

WHEN IS MODE LESS THAN MEAN?, MORE THAN?: In Example 6, mode < mean. But this is not a universal rule — in other distributions the mode may equal or exceed the mean. The relationship depends on the shape of the data.

CHOOSING BETWEEN MODE AND MEAN: When you want the 'most frequent' outcome — the most common score, the most popular shoe size, the most demanded item — mode is the right measure. When you want the average overall — the average marks, the average income — mean is appropriate. Both are 'averages' in everyday language, but they answer different questions.

ERROR ALERT — 'I used the class mark of the modal class as the mode': A frequent mistake. The class mark 47.5 of the modal class 40-55 in Example 6 is NOT the mode. You must apply the formula, which gave 52. The formula accounts for the neighbouring classes' frequencies.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'Highest frequency directly gives the mode': The highest frequency only gives the modal CLASS. The mode is a specific value inside that class, found using the formula.

REMARK — unequal class sizes: Mode can also be calculated for grouped data with unequal class sizes, though the formula changes slightly. Class 10 problems restrict to equal class sizes.

In a grouped frequency distribution, it is not possible to determine the mode by looking at the frequencies. Here, we can only locate a class with the maximum frequency, called the modal class. The mode is a value inside the modal class, and is given by the formula:

Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h

where l = lower limit of the modal class,
h = size of the class interval (assuming all class sizes to be equal),
f₁ = frequency of the modal class,
f₀ = frequency of the class preceding the modal class,
f₂ = frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.

Let us consider the following examples to illustrate the use of this formula.

Example 5: A survey conducted on 20 households in a locality by a group of students resulted in the following frequency table for the number of family members in a household:

| Family size | 1-3 | 3-5 | 5-7 | 7-9 | 9-11 |
| Number of families | 7 | 8 | 2 | 2 | 1 |

Find the mode of this data.

Solution: Here the maximum class frequency is 8, and the class corresponding to this frequency is 3-5. So, the modal class is 3-5.

Now
modal class = 3-5, lower limit (l) of modal class = 3, class size (h) = 2
frequency (f₁) of the modal class = 8,
frequency (f₀) of class preceding the modal class = 7,
frequency (f₂) of class succeeding the modal class = 2.

Now, let us substitute these values in the formula:

Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h
     = 3 + ((8 − 7) / (2×8 − 7 − 2)) × 2
     = 3 + 2/7
     = 3.286

Therefore, the mode of the data above is 3.286.

Example 6: The marks distribution of 30 students in a mathematics examination are given in Table 13.3 of Example 1. Find the mode of this data. Also compare and interpret the mode and the mean.

Solution: Refer to Table 13.3 of Example 1. Since the maximum number of students (i.e., 7) have got marks in the interval 40-55, the modal class is 40-55. Therefore,

the lower limit (l) of the modal class = 40,
the class size (h) = 15,
the frequency (f₁) of modal class = 7,
the frequency (f₀) of the class preceding the modal class = 3,
the frequency (f₂) of the class succeeding the modal class = 6.

Now, using the formula:

Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h,

we get Mode = 40 + ((7 − 3) / (14 − 6 − 3)) × 15 = 52

So, the mode marks is 52.

Now, from Example 1, you know that the mean marks is 62.

So, the maximum number of students obtained 52 marks, while on an average a student obtained 62 marks.

Remarks:
1. In Example 6, the mode is less than the mean. But for some other problems it may be equal or more than the mean also.
2. It depends upon the demand of the situation whether we are interested in finding the average marks obtained by the students or the average of the marks obtained by most of the students. In the first situation, the mean is required and in the second situation, the mode is required.

recall_questions.prompt: A distribution of electricity-consumption has class intervals 65-85, 85-105, 105-125, 125-145, 145-165, 165-185, 185-205 with frequencies 4, 5, 13, 20, 14, 7, 4. Identify the modal class and compute the mode.

recall_questions.answer: Within the modal class, we do not know the exact distribution of individual values. However, the frequencies of the adjacent classes tell us about the shape of the distribution at the class boundaries. If the preceding class has a high frequency (f₀ is large and close to f₁), many observations from the modal class are likely concentrated near its lower boundary — so the formula shifts the mode toward l. If the succeeding class has a high frequency (f₂ is large), observations are more concentrated toward the upper boundary. The formula l + ((f₁−f₀)/(2f₁−f₀−f₂)) × h captures this asymmetry by giving more weight to the boundary of the higher-frequency neighbour.
recall_questions.prompt: Why does the mode formula use f₀ and f₂ (the neighbouring class frequencies) rather than just f₁ to locate the mode within the modal class?

topics.modified_chunk:
INTRODUCTION: These six exercise questions practise finding the mode of grouped data and comparing it with the mean. In each case, your workflow is: (1) identify the modal class, (2) list l, h, f₀, f₁, f₂, (3) apply the formula, (4) where asked, also compute the mean and interpret the comparison.

STRATEGY GUIDE — for each question:

- Q1 (patient ages, class size 10): Modal class is 35-45 (frequency 23). Also compute the mean (use Step-Deviation with a = 30 or 40, h = 10) and compare: which is higher, and what does each tell you about the age profile of admitted patients?

- Q2 (component lifetimes, class size 20): Modal class is 60-80 (frequency 61). Straight formula application.

- Q3 (household expenditure, class size 500): Modal class is 1500-2000 (frequency 40). Also compute the mean — with large xᵢ values and equal class widths, Step-Deviation is most efficient.

- Q4 (teacher-student ratio, UNEVEN frequencies including ZEROS): Modal class is 30-35 (frequency 10). Be careful: two class intervals have frequency 0 (40-45, 45-50). Compare mode and mean — the mean is skewed by the small cluster at 50-55.

- Q5 (runs scored, class size 1000): Modal class is 4000-5000 (frequency 18). Simple formula application.

- Q6 (number of cars, class size 10): Modal class is 40-50 (frequency 20). Note that 60-70 and 10-20 both have relatively high frequencies (15, 14), so f₀ and f₂ are not dramatically different — the mode will fall roughly in the middle of 40-50.

WORKED STRATEGY DEMO (Q1, complete): Ages of patients admitted in a hospital.

| Age (in years) | 5-15 | 15-25 | 25-35 | 35-45 | 45-55 | 55-65 |
| Number of patients | 6 | 11 | 21 | 23 | 14 | 5 |

Step 1: Modal class is 35-45 (max frequency = 23).
Step 2: l = 35, h = 10, f₁ = 23, f₀ = 21, f₂ = 14.
Step 3: Mode = 35 + ((23 − 21) / (46 − 21 − 14)) × 10 = 35 + (2/11) × 10 = 35 + 1.82 = 36.82 years.

Now the mean. Class marks: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Take a = 30, h = 10. uᵢ = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. fᵢuᵢ = −12, −11, 0, 23, 28, 15. Σfᵢuᵢ = 43. Σfᵢ = 80.

Mean = 30 + 10 × (43/80) = 30 + 5.375 = 35.375 years.

Interpretation: The mode (36.82) and the mean (35.375) are both in the 35-45 age bracket, so the 'typical' and 'average' admitted patient are close to each other — a sign that the age distribution is roughly balanced around this range.

PARTIALLY FADED DEMO (Q4, you complete the mean): Teacher-student ratio in higher secondary schools.

| Number of students per teacher | 15-20 | 20-25 | 25-30 | 30-35 | 35-40 | 40-45 | 45-50 | 50-55 |
| Number of states/U.T. | 3 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 2 |

Mode: Modal class 30-35. l = 30, h = 5, f₁ = 10, f₀ = 9, f₂ = 3. Apply: Mode = 30 + (1/8) × 5 = 30 + 0.625 = 30.625.

Mean: You work out — class marks 17.5, 22.5, 27.5, 32.5, 37.5, 42.5, 47.5, 52.5. Pick a = 32.5, h = 5. Work through uᵢ, fᵢuᵢ, Σfᵢuᵢ, and finally mean. Interpret: two small states with ratios in 50-55 pull the mean higher than the mode.

ERROR ALERT — common pitfalls in mode problems:
1. Forgetting to check for equal class sizes before applying the formula.
2. Swapping f₀ and f₂ — always read f₀ = preceding class, f₂ = succeeding class.
3. Using 2f₁ − f₀ − f₂ wrongly as 2f₁ + f₀ + f₂ or 2(f₁ − f₀ − f₂).

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'mode and mean should always agree': They seldom do exactly, and the extent of their difference tells you something about the shape of the data. Large differences indicate skewness; equal values indicate symmetry.

CHECK-IN before you begin: For each question, first write the three-column rough table (l, h, f₀/f₁/f₂) before plugging into the formula. This prevents most arithmetic errors.

Each problem requires identifying the modal class from the frequency column, extracting f₀, f₁, f₂, l, h, substituting into the formula, and computing the mode. recall_questions.answer:
Step 1 — identify modal class: maximum frequency is 23 in age group 35-45. Modal class = 35-45.
Step 2 — extract: l = 35, f₁ = 23, f₀ = 21 (class 25-35), f₂ = 14 (class 45-55), h = 10.
Step 3 — apply formula:
Mode = 35 + ((23 − 21) / (2×23 − 21 − 14)) × 10
= 35 + (2 / (46 − 35)) × 10
= 35 + (2/11) × 10
= 35 + 1.82 ≈ 36.8 years.
Therefore the modal age is approximately 36.8 years.
recall_questions.prompt: Find the mode for the following hospital admissions distribution: age groups 5-15, 15-25, 25-35, 35-45, 45-55, 55-65 with frequencies 6, 11, 21, 23, 14, 5.

recall_questions.answer: The mode (36.8) is slightly larger than the mean (35.37). In a distribution, if mode > mean, the distribution is slightly left-skewed (the tail extends toward lower values, pulling the mean below the mode). The difference is small (about 1.4 years), so the distribution is approximately symmetric. We can also use the empirical relation as a partial check: 3 × Median ≈ Mode + 2 × Mean = 36.8 + 2×35.37 = 107.54, so Median ≈ 35.85. A median of 35.85 sitting between 35.37 (mean) and 36.8 (mode) is consistent with a mildly left-skewed pattern.
recall_questions.prompt: For the distribution in TR1 above, the mean was separately computed as 35.37 years. Verify whether this is consistent with the mode of 36.8 years. What does the comparison suggest about the shape of the distribution?

recall_questions.answer: The mode (65.6 hours) is more appropriate for the factory manager's question. 'How long do most components last' is asking for the most common failure time — which is exactly what the mode measures (the modal class 60-80 has the highest frequency, meaning the most components fail in this range). modules.detailed_summary: Module 2 teaches how to find the mode of grouped frequency data. In ungrouped data, the mode is the observation with the highest frequency — a direct read-off. In grouped data, frequencies attach to class intervals rather than individual values, so instead of a single mode value the student first identifies the modal class (the class with the highest frequency) and then interpolates within it using the formula Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h. Each symbol is carefully defined: l is the lower limit of the modal class, f₁ its frequency, f₀ and f₂ the frequencies of the immediately preceding and succeeding classes, and h the uniform class width. Two worked examples — one with a modal class near the left boundary, one with closely-competing neighbours — demonstrate the formula in detail. The module closes with Exercise 13.2 practice, including an important comparison between the computed mode and the mean of the same distribution.

modules.summary: Module 3 completes the chapter's central toolkit by adding the median to the mean and mode already studied. The module opens with a recap of the ungrouped median from Class IX, then builds cumulative frequency distributions of both the less-than and more-than-or-equal-to types. These tables allow the student to locate the median class — the interval that brackets the n/2 th observation — and then apply the linear interpolation formula Median = l + ((n/2 − cf)/f) × h to pinpoint the median within that class. Two worked examples illustrate the formula directly, including a harder case where the median is given and missing frequencies must be found by combining the formula with the total-frequency condition. A culminating REVIEW topic shows when to prefer mean, median, or mode, and derives the empirical relation 3 × Median ≈ Mode + 2 × Mean. The module closes with Exercise 13.3 mixed practice, which asks for all three measures from a single distribution and their comparison.

topics.summary: The median of ungrouped data is found by locating the middle position in the cumulative frequency column: for n even, average the n/2-th and (n/2+1)-th observations; for n odd, the median is the ((n+1)/2)-th observation.
topics.brief_summary: The median of ungrouped data is the middle observation — the ((n+1)/2)th for odd n, or the average of the (n/2)th and ((n/2)+1)th for even n.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: The mean balances all observations; the mode tracks the most frequent value. The median takes a different approach — it locates the middle-most observation, the value that splits the data set cleanly into two equal halves. Before tackling grouped median in the next topic, let us first reactivate the ungrouped version from Class IX.

RECALL: The median is a measure of central tendency that gives the value of the middle-most observation. For ungrouped data, the procedure is:
  Step 1: Arrange the observations in ascending order.
  Step 2: If the total count n is odd, the median is the ((n+1)/2)th observation.
           If n is even, the median is the average of the (n/2)th and the ((n/2)+1)th observations.

WORKED EXAMPLE (complete): Find the median of marks (out of 50) obtained by 100 students in a test:

| Marks obtained | 20 | 29 | 28 | 33 | 42 | 38 | 43 | 25 |
| Number of students | 6 | 28 | 24 | 15 | 2 | 4 | 1 | 20 |

Solution:

Step 1: Arrange the marks in ascending order and prepare the frequency table.

Table 13.9
| Marks obtained | Number of students (Frequency) |
| 20 | 6 |
| 25 | 20 |
| 28 | 24 |
| 29 | 28 |
| 33 | 15 |
| 38 | 4 |
| 42 | 2 |
| 43 | 1 |
| Total | 100 |

Step 2: n = 100, which is even. So the median equals the average of the (n/2)th = 50th and the ((n/2)+1)th = 51st observations.

Step 3: Use running totals to locate the 50th and 51st observations.

Table 13.10
| Marks obtained | Cumulative count |
| 20 | 6 |
| upto 25 | 6 + 20 = 26 |
| upto 28 | 26 + 24 = 50 |
| upto 29 | 50 + 28 = 78 |
| upto 33 | 78 + 15 = 93 |
| upto 38 | 93 + 4 = 97 |
| upto 42 | 97 + 2 = 99 |
| upto 43 | 99 + 1 = 100 |

We rewrite this alongside the original frequency column — this new column is the cumulative frequency.

Table 13.11
| Marks obtained | Number of students | Cumulative frequency |
| 20 | 6 | 6 |
| 25 | 20 | 26 |
| 28 | 24 | 50 |
| 29 | 28 | 78 |
| 33 | 15 | 93 |
| 38 | 4 | 97 |
| 42 | 2 | 99 |
| 43 | 1 | 100 |

Step 4: Read off the 50th and 51st observations. The cumulative frequency reaches 50 exactly at marks = 28. So the 50th student has 28 marks. The 51st student is in the next row, where cumulative frequency jumps to 78 — so the 51st student has 29 marks.

Step 5: Apply the even-n rule.

  Median = (28 + 29)/2 = 28.5

WHY THIS STEP? The cumulative frequency column acts as a positional index — it tells us, for any given mark value, how many students scored up to (and including) that value. Using it to find the 50th student is far faster than writing out all 100 observations.

INTERPRETATION: The median mark is 28.5. This means about 50% of the students obtained marks less than 28.5, and the other 50% obtained marks greater than 28.5.

ERROR ALERT — mixing up odd-n and even-n rules: If n had been 99 instead of 100, the median would be the single middle observation: the ((99+1)/2)th = 50th observation, not an average.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'the median is always a value that actually occurs in the data': Not necessarily. For n = 100, the median could be the average of two different values (like (28+29)/2 = 28.5) — a value not present in any student's actual score.

KEY IDEA FOR NEXT TOPIC: The cumulative frequency column was the tool that made finding the middle observation efficient. In the next topic we extend this to grouped data, where cumulative frequency becomes central.

topics.original_chunk:
As you have studied in Class IX, the median is a measure of central tendency which gives the value of the middle-most observation in the data. Recall that for finding the median of ungrouped data, we first arrange the data values of the observations in ascending order. Then, if n is odd, the median is the ((n+1)/2)th observation. And, if n is even, then the median will be the average of the (n/2)th and the ((n/2)+1)th observations.

Suppose, we have to find the median of the following data, which gives the marks, out of 50, obtained by 100 students in a test:

| Marks obtained | 20 | 29 | 28 | 33 | 42 | 38 | 43 | 25 |
| Number of students | 6 | 28 | 24 | 15 | 2 | 4 | 1 | 20 |

First, we arrange the marks in ascending order and prepare a frequency table as follows:

Table 13.9
| Marks obtained | Number of students (Frequency) |
| 20 | 6 |
| 25 | 20 |
| 28 | 24 |
| 29 | 28 |
| 33 | 15 |
| 38 | 4 |
| 42 | 2 |
| 43 | 1 |
| Total | 100 |

Here n = 100, which is even. The median will be the average of the (n/2)th and the ((n/2)+1)th observations, i.e., the 50th and 51st observations. To find these observations, we proceed as follows:

Table 13.10
| Marks obtained | Number of students |
| 20 | 6 |
| upto 25 | 6 + 20 = 26 |
| upto 28 | 26 + 24 = 50 |
| upto 29 | 50 + 28 = 78 |
| upto 33 | 78 + 15 = 93 |
| upto 38 | 93 + 4 = 97 |
| upto 42 | 97 + 2 = 99 |
| upto 43 | 99 + 1 = 100 |

Now we add another column depicting this information to the frequency table above and name it as cumulative frequency column.

Table 13.11
| Marks obtained | Number of students | Cumulative frequency |
| 20 | 6 | 6 |
| 25 | 20 | 26 |
| 28 | 24 | 50 |
| 29 | 28 | 78 |
| 33 | 15 | 93 |
| 38 | 4 | 97 |
| 42 | 2 | 99 |
| 43 | 1 | 100 |

From the table above, we see that:
50th observation is 28 (Why?)
51st observation is 29

So, Median = (28 + 29)/2 = 28.5

Remark: The part of Table 13.11 consisting Column 1 and Column 3 is known as Cumulative Frequency Table. The median marks 28.5 conveys the information that about 50% students obtained marks less than 28.5 and another 50% students obtained marks more than 28.5.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In ungrouped data, cumulative frequency helped us locate the middle observation in one column. In grouped data, cumulative frequency plays an even bigger role — it is the gateway to finding the median class. Let us build the tool carefully before applying it.

SETUP: Consider a grouped frequency distribution of marks (out of 100) obtained by 53 students in an examination.

Table 13.12
| Marks | Number of students |
| 0-10 | 5 |
| 10-20 | 3 |
| 20-30 | 4 |
| 30-40 | 3 |
| 40-50 | 3 |
| 50-60 | 4 |
| 60-70 | 7 |
| 70-80 | 9 |
| 80-90 | 7 |
| 90-100 | 8 |

CORE — 'less than type' cumulative frequency: Let us answer a sequence of questions.

Q: How many students scored marks less than 10? A: Clearly 5 — the only interval below 10 is 0-10, with 5 students.

Q: How many scored less than 20? A: The students with marks less than 20 are those in the 0-10 class PLUS those in the 10-20 class. Total = 5 + 3 = 8. We say the cumulative frequency of class 10-20 is 8.

Continuing similarly, we build the 'less than' cumulative distribution.

Table 13.13
| Marks obtained | Number of students (Cumulative frequency) |
| Less than 10 | 5 |
| Less than 20 | 5 + 3 = 8 |
| Less than 30 | 8 + 4 = 12 |
| Less than 40 | 12 + 3 = 15 |
| Less than 50 | 15 + 3 = 18 |
| Less than 60 | 18 + 4 = 22 |
| Less than 70 | 22 + 7 = 29 |
| Less than 80 | 29 + 9 = 38 |
| Less than 90 | 38 + 7 = 45 |
| Less than 100 | 45 + 8 = 53 |

This is called the cumulative frequency distribution of the less than type. Notice that the boundaries 10, 20, 30, ..., 100 used here are the UPPER limits of the original class intervals.

CORE — 'more than or equal to' cumulative frequency: We can build the same idea from the other end.

All 53 students scored more than or equal to 0 (trivially). Since 5 students fall in class 0-10, there are 53 − 5 = 48 students with marks more than or equal to 10. Then 48 − 3 = 45 students with marks more than or equal to 20, then 45 − 4 = 41, and so on.

Table 13.14
| Marks obtained | Number of students (Cumulative frequency) |
| More than or equal to 0 | 53 |
| More than or equal to 10 | 53 − 5 = 48 |
| More than or equal to 20 | 48 − 3 = 45 |
| More than or equal to 30 | 45 − 4 = 41 |
| More than or equal to 40 | 41 − 3 = 38 |
| More than or equal to 50 | 38 − 3 = 35 |
| More than or equal to 60 | 35 − 4 = 31 |
| More than or equal to 70 | 31 − 7 = 24 |
| More than or equal to 80 | 24 − 9 = 15 |
| More than or equal to 90 | 15 − 7 = 8 |

This is the cumulative frequency distribution of the more than type. The boundaries 0, 10, 20, ..., 90 used here are the LOWER limits of the original class intervals.

WHY TWO TYPES? The 'less than' type is used most often for median calculation (the next topic). The 'more than or equal to' type is more natural when you want to count how many observations reach or exceed a threshold (like 'how many students scored 60 or above'). Both contain the same information — one can always be converted to the other using the total count n.

WORKED EXAMPLE (self-check on conversion, partially faded): Using Table 13.13, the cumulative frequency of 'less than 60' is 22. Using Table 13.14, the cumulative frequency of 'more than or equal to 60' is 31. You verify: 22 + 31 = 53, which equals n. This identity — (less than cf at upper limit) + (more than or equal cf at same lower limit of next class) = n — holds for every class boundary.

ERROR ALERT — confusing upper vs lower limits: A common mistake is to write 'less than 10 gives cumulative frequency 5' but then use the class 10-20 as 'less than 20' (instead of upper limit 20). Always anchor each row to the correct LIMIT — upper for less than, lower for more than or equal to.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'cumulative frequency resets at each class': It does not. It is strictly non-decreasing for less than type and non-increasing for more than or equal type. If it decreases (in less than type) or increases (in more than or equal type), you have an arithmetic mistake.

KEY IDEA FOR NEXT TOPIC: The less than type cumulative frequency distribution is the tool we will use to locate the median CLASS of grouped data — the class inside which the median lives.

CHECK: Using Table 13.13, how many students scored less than 70 marks? Using Table 13.14, how many scored 40 or above? Verify your two answers obey the identity (less than cf at 70) + (more than or equal cf at 70) = 53.
topics.original_chunk:
Now, let us see how to obtain the median of grouped data, through the following situation.

Consider a grouped frequency distribution of marks obtained, out of 100, by 53 students, in a certain examination, as follows:

Table 13.12
| Marks | Number of students |
| 0-10 | 5 |
| 10-20 | 3 |
| 20-30 | 4 |
| 30-40 | 3 |
| 40-50 | 3 |
| 50-60 | 4 |
| 60-70 | 7 |
| 70-80 | 9 |
| 80-90 | 7 |
| 90-100 | 8 |

From the table above, try to answer the following questions:

How many students have scored marks less than 10? The answer is clearly 5.

How many students have scored less than 20 marks? Observe that the number of students who have scored less than 20 include the number of students who have scored marks from 0-10 as well as the number of students who have scored marks from 10-20. So, the total number of students with marks less than 20 is 5 + 3, i.e., 8. We say that the cumulative frequency of the class 10-20 is 8.

Similarly, we can compute the cumulative frequencies of the other classes, i.e., the number of students with marks less than 30, less than 40, ..., less than 100. We give them in Table 13.13 given below:

Table 13.13
| Marks obtained | Number of students (Cumulative frequency) |
| Less than 10 | 5 |
| Less than 20 | 5 + 3 = 8 |
| Less than 30 | 8 + 4 = 12 |
| Less than 40 | 12 + 3 = 15 |
| Less than 50 | 15 + 3 = 18 |
| Less than 60 | 18 + 4 = 22 |
| Less than 70 | 22 + 7 = 29 |
| Less than 80 | 29 + 9 = 38 |
| Less than 90 | 38 + 7 = 45 |
| Less than 100 | 45 + 8 = 53 |

The distribution given above is called the cumulative frequency distribution of the less than type. Here 10, 20, 30, ... 100, are the upper limits of the respective class intervals.

We can similarly make the table for the number of students with scores, more than or equal to 0, more than or equal to 10, more than or equal to 20, and so on. From Table 13.12, we observe that all 53 students have scored marks more than or equal to 0. Since there are 5 students scoring marks in the interval 0-10, this means that there are 53 − 5 = 48 students getting more than or equal to 10 marks. Continuing in the same manner, we get the number of students scoring 20 or above as 48 − 3 = 45, 30 or above as 45 − 4 = 41, and so on, as shown in Table 13.14.

Table 13.14
| Marks obtained | Number of students (Cumulative frequency) |
| More than or equal to 0 | 53 |
| More than or equal to 10 | 53 − 5 = 48 |
| More than or equal to 20 | 48 − 3 = 45 |
| More than or equal to 30 | 45 − 4 = 41 |
| More than or equal to 40 | 41 − 3 = 38 |
| More than or equal to 50 | 38 − 3 = 35 |
| More than or equal to 60 | 35 − 4 = 31 |
| More than or equal to 70 | 31 − 7 = 24 |
| More than or equal to 80 | 24 − 9 = 15 |
| More than or equal to 90 | 15 − 7 = 8 |

The table above is called a cumulative frequency distribution of the more than type. Here 0, 10, 20, ..., 90 give the lower limits of the respective class intervals.
concept_bullets: Less-than cumulative frequency — add class frequencies from the top: 'less than 10' = 5, 'less than 20' = 5+3 = 8, 'less than 30' = 8+4 = 12, continuing until the last upper boundary gives n = 53.
More-than-or-equal-to cumulative frequency — start at n = 53 and subtract each class frequency in turn: 'at least 0' = 53, 'at least 10' = 53−5 = 48, 'at least 20' = 48−3 = 45.
Complementary identity — for any class boundary b: (less-than cf at upper limit b) + (more-than-or-equal-to cf at same lower limit b) = n; verify: 22 + 31 = 53 at the boundary 60.
topics.detailed_summary: For grouped data, individual values are unknown, so the median requires a new tool: the cumulative frequency distribution. This topic builds both types from the 53-student marks distribution. The less-than type answers 'how many students scored less than X?' for each upper class boundary X: starting from 5 (less than 10), each row adds the next class frequency to the previous total, reaching 53 at the last row. The more-than-or-equal-to type answers the complementary question from the lower boundaries, subtracting each frequency in turn from 53. The two distributions are complementary — at any boundary, their sum equals n = 53. The less-than type will be used in the next topic to locate the median class.
important_points: How many students have scored marks less than 10? The answer is clearly 5.

How many students have scored less than 20 marks? Observe that the number of students who have scored less than 20 include the number of students who have scored marks from 0-10 as well as the number of students who have scored marks from 10-20.
cumulative frequency of the class 10-20 is 8.

recall_questions.answer:
| Class | Frequency | Cumulative frequency (less than) |
| 0-5 | 10 | 10 |
| 5-10 | 12 | 10+12 = 22 |
| 10-15 | 8 | 22+8 = 30 |
| 15-20 | 5 | 30+5 = 35 |

So: less than 5 → 10, less than 10 → 22, less than 15 → 30, less than 20 → 35 (= n = total).
