recall_questions.answer:
More-than-or-equal-to table:
| At least | Cumulative frequency |
| 0 | 35 |
| 5 | 35−10 = 25 |
| 10 | 25−12 = 13 |
| 15 | 13−8 = 5 |

Verification at boundary 10:
- Less than 10 = 22 (from TR1)
- More than or equal to 10 = 13 (from above)
- Sum = 22 + 13 = 35 = n ✓
The complementary identity holds.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: With cumulative frequency in hand, we can now find the median of grouped data. The plan is: locate the class that contains the middle observation (the median class), then use a formula to pinpoint the median value inside that class.

RECALL: In ungrouped data, the median was a specific observation. In grouped data, the observation is hidden inside a class interval — so we find the median class first, then interpolate within it.

CORE — finding the median class: Start with the combined frequency and less-than cumulative frequency table.

Table 13.15
| Marks | Number of students (f) | Cumulative frequency (cf) |
| 0-10 | 5 | 5 |
| 10-20 | 3 | 8 |
| 20-30 | 4 | 12 |
| 30-40 | 3 | 15 |
| 40-50 | 3 | 18 |
| 50-60 | 4 | 22 |
| 60-70 | 7 | 29 |
| 70-80 | 9 | 38 |
| 80-90 | 7 | 45 |
| 90-100 | 8 | 53 |

Compute n/2. For this distribution, n = 53, so n/2 = 26.5. Now scan down the cf column: find the class whose cf is GREATER than (and nearest to) n/2. Here, cf = 22 (for class 50-60) is still less than 26.5, but cf = 29 (for class 60-70) crosses 26.5. So the median class is 60-70.

CORE — the median formula:

  Median = l + ((n/2 − cf) / f) × h

where
  l  = lower limit of the median class,
  n  = number of observations (total count),
  cf = cumulative frequency of the class PRECEDING the median class,
  f  = frequency of the median class,
  h  = class size (assuming all class sizes equal).

APPLYING IT: For the median class 60-70, we have l = 60, cf = 22 (the cf of class 50-60, which precedes 60-70), f = 7, h = 10.

  Median = 60 + ((26.5 − 22)/7) × 10 = 60 + 45/7 = 66.4

WHY THIS STEP? The formula treats frequency inside the median class as uniformly distributed, then linearly interpolates to the position where exactly n/2 observations fall below. (n/2 − cf) counts how many 'missing' observations we need beyond the previous class; dividing by f tells us the fractional position within the median class.

INTERPRETATION: About half the students have scored marks less than 66.4, and the other half have scored marks more than 66.4.

ERROR ALERT — cf in the formula refers to the class PRECEDING the median class, not the median class itself. Picking cf = 29 (the cf of 60-70 itself) would give a wrong answer. Always use the cf just below.

WORKED EXAMPLE 7 (complete — less-than-type input): A survey of 51 girls of Class X recorded heights as follows:

| Height (in cm) | Number of girls |
| Less than 140 | 4 |
| Less than 145 | 11 |
| Less than 150 | 29 |
| Less than 155 | 40 |
| Less than 160 | 46 |
| Less than 165 | 51 |

Find the median height.

Solution:

Step 1: The given data is already cumulative frequency of less than type. The boundaries 140, 145, 150, ..., 165 are UPPER limits of class intervals. So the classes are Below 140, 140-145, 145-150, 150-155, 155-160, 160-165.

Step 2: Recover per-class frequencies by successive subtraction. For instance, the interval 140-145 has frequency 11 − 4 = 7. Similarly 145-150 has 29 − 11 = 18, and so on.

Table 13.16
| Class intervals | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| Below 140 | 4 | 4 |
| 140-145 | 7 | 11 |
| 145-150 | 18 | 29 |
| 150-155 | 11 | 40 |
| 155-160 | 6 | 46 |
| 160-165 | 5 | 51 |

Step 3: n = 51, so n/2 = 25.5. The cf first exceeds 25.5 at the class 145-150 (cf = 29). Median class = 145-150.

Step 4: Ingredients. l = 145, cf = 11 (from preceding class 140-145), f = 18, h = 5.

Step 5: Apply the formula.

  Median = 145 + ((25.5 − 11)/18) × 5 = 145 + 72.5/18 = 149.03 cm

The median height of the girls is 149.03 cm. About 50% of the girls are less than this height, and 50% are taller.

WORKED EXAMPLE 8 (partially faded — find missing frequencies): The median of the following data is 525. The total frequency is 100. Find x and y.

| Class intervals | Frequency |
| 0-100 | 2 |
| 100-200 | 5 |
| 200-300 | x |
| 300-400 | 12 |
| 400-500 | 17 |
| 500-600 | 20 |
| 600-700 | y |
| 700-800 | 9 |
| 800-900 | 7 |
| 900-1000 | 4 |

Solution:

Step 1: Build cumulative frequencies keeping x and y symbolic.

| Class intervals | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| 0-100 | 2 | 2 |
| 100-200 | 5 | 7 |
| 200-300 | x | 7 + x |
| 300-400 | 12 | 19 + x |
| 400-500 | 17 | 36 + x |
| 500-600 | 20 | 56 + x |
| 600-700 | y | 56 + x + y |
| 700-800 | 9 | 65 + x + y |
| 800-900 | 7 | 72 + x + y |
| 900-1000 | 4 | 76 + x + y |

Step 2: Total frequency condition. n = 100, so 76 + x + y = 100 ⇒ x + y = 24.  ...(1)

Step 3: The given median is 525, which lies in 500-600. So the median class is 500-600. Read ingredients: l = 500, f = 20, cf (of preceding class 400-500) = 36 + x, h = 100.

Step 4: Apply the formula.

  525 = 500 + ((50 − (36 + x))/20) × 100
  525 − 500 = (14 − x) × 5
  25 = 70 − 5x
  5x = 45
  x = 9

Step 5: Substitute x = 9 in equation (1): 9 + y = 24 ⇒ y = 15.

Therefore x = 9, y = 15.

WHY THIS STEP? When the median is given and frequencies are unknown, the median formula plus the total frequency condition give a 2×2 system in the unknowns — enough to solve.

ERROR ALERT — identifying the median class when the median is given: Do not recompute n/2 and search for the median class by cumulative frequency; use the given median value (525) to spot the interval it falls into (500-600). The cumulative frequency check comes AFTER you have identified the class.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'the formula's l should be the class mark': l is the LOWER LIMIT, not the class mark. For class 500-600, l = 500 (not 550).

CHECK: In Example 7, what would the median height become if the class 145-150 had frequency 20 instead of 18, with n and all other frequencies adjusted so that the median class stays the same?
topics.original_chunk:
Now, to find the median of grouped data, we can make use of any of these cumulative frequency distributions.

Let us combine Tables 13.12 and 13.13 to get Table 13.15 given below:

Table 13.15
| Marks | Number of students (f) | Cumulative frequency (cf) |
| 0-10 | 5 | 5 |
| 10-20 | 3 | 8 |
| 20-30 | 4 | 12 |
| 30-40 | 3 | 15 |
| 40-50 | 3 | 18 |
| 50-60 | 4 | 22 |
| 60-70 | 7 | 29 |
| 70-80 | 9 | 38 |
| 80-90 | 7 | 45 |
| 90-100 | 8 | 53 |

Now in a grouped data, we may not be able to find the middle observation by looking at the cumulative frequencies as the middle observation will be some value in a class interval. It is, therefore, necessary to find the value inside a class that divides the whole distribution into two halves. But which class should this be?

To find this class, we find the cumulative frequencies of all the classes and n/2. We now locate the class whose cumulative frequency is greater than (and nearest to) n/2. This is called the median class. In the distribution above, n = 53. So, n/2 = 26.5. Now 60-70 is the class whose cumulative frequency 29 is greater than (and nearest to) n/2, i.e., 26.5.

Therefore, 60-70 is the median class.

After finding the median class, we use the following formula for calculating the median.

Median = l + ((n/2 − cf) / f) × h,

where l = lower limit of median class,
n = number of observations,
cf = cumulative frequency of class preceding the median class,
f = frequency of median class,
h = class size (assuming class size to be equal).

Substituting the values n/2 = 26.5, l = 60, cf = 22, f = 7, h = 10 in the formula above, we get

Median = 60 + ((26.5 − 22)/7) × 10
       = 60 + 45/7
       = 66.4

So, about half the students have scored marks less than 66.4, and the other half have scored marks more than 66.4.

Example 7: A survey regarding the heights (in cm) of 51 girls of Class X of a school was conducted and the following data was obtained:

| Height (in cm) | Number of girls |
| Less than 140 | 4 |
| Less than 145 | 11 |
| Less than 150 | 29 |
| Less than 155 | 40 |
| Less than 160 | 46 |
| Less than 165 | 51 |

Find the median height.

Solution: To calculate the median height, we need to find the class intervals and their corresponding frequencies.

The given distribution being of the less than type, 140, 145, 150, ..., 165 give the upper limits of the corresponding class intervals. So, the classes should be below 140, 140-145, 145-150, ..., 160-165. Observe that from the given distribution, we find that there are 4 girls with height less than 140, i.e., the frequency of class interval below 140 is 4. Now, there are 11 girls with heights less than 145 and 4 girls with height less than 140. Therefore, the number of girls with height in the interval 140-145 is 11 − 4 = 7. Similarly, the frequency of 145-150 is 29 − 11 = 18, for 150-155, it is 40 − 29 = 11, and so on. So, our frequency distribution table with the given cumulative frequencies becomes:

Table 13.16
| Class intervals | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| Below 140 | 4 | 4 |
| 140-145 | 7 | 11 |
| 145-150 | 18 | 29 |
| 150-155 | 11 | 40 |
| 155-160 | 6 | 46 |
| 160-165 | 5 | 51 |

Now n = 51. So, n/2 = 51/2 = 25.5. This observation lies in the class 145-150. Then,
l (the lower limit) = 145,
cf (the cumulative frequency of the class preceding 145-150) = 11,
f (the frequency of the median class 145-150) = 18,
h (the class size) = 5.

Using the formula, Median = l + ((n/2 − cf)/f) × h, we have

Median = 145 + ((25.5 − 11)/18) × 5
       = 145 + 72.5/18
       = 149.03.

So, the median height of the girls is 149.03 cm.

This means that the height of about 50% of the girls is less than this height, and 50% are taller than this height.

Example 8: The median of the following data is 525. Find the values of x and y, if the total frequency is 100.

| Class intervals | Frequency |
| 0-100 | 2 |
| 100-200 | 5 |
| 200-300 | x |
| 300-400 | 12 |
| 400-500 | 17 |
| 500-600 | 20 |
| 600-700 | y |
| 700-800 | 9 |
| 800-900 | 7 |
| 900-1000 | 4 |

Solution:
| Class intervals | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| 0-100 | 2 | 2 |
| 100-200 | 5 | 7 |
| 200-300 | x | 7 + x |
| 300-400 | 12 | 19 + x |
| 400-500 | 17 | 36 + x |
| 500-600 | 20 | 56 + x |
| 600-700 | y | 56 + x + y |
| 700-800 | 9 | 65 + x + y |
| 800-900 | 7 | 72 + x + y |
| 900-1000 | 4 | 76 + x + y |

It is given that n = 100
So, 76 + x + y = 100, i.e., x + y = 24  ... (1)
The median is 525, which lies in the class 500-600
So, l = 500, f = 20, cf = 36 + x, h = 100

Using the formula: Median = l + ((n/2 − cf)/f) × h, we get

525 = 500 + ((50 − 36 − x)/20) × 100
i.e., 525 − 500 = (14 − x) × 5
i.e., 25 = 70 − 5x
i.e., 5x = 70 − 25 = 45
So, x = 9

Therefore, from (1), we get 9 + y = 24
i.e., y = 15

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: You now have three tools for summarising a data set — the mean, the median, and the mode. Each tells a different story, and none of them is 'the right one' in all cases. This topic is about choosing the tool that fits the question at hand.

RECALL: Mean = average of all observations; median = middle-most observation; mode = most frequent observation (or modal-class interpolation for grouped data).

CORE — when to prefer the MEAN: The mean is the most commonly used measure because it takes every observation into account and sits between the smallest and largest values. This makes it ideal for COMPARING two or more distributions. For example, comparing the mean marks of students from different schools in the same exam tells us which school performed better overall.

LIMITATION — extreme values skew the mean: Mean is pulled by outliers. If one class interval has a tiny frequency (say 2) while five others are around 20, the mean will be dragged off-centre and no longer represents the bulk of the data. In such skewed situations, mean is not a good representative.

CORE — when to prefer the MEDIAN: When individual observations are not important and you want a 'typical' value robust to extremes, the median is better. Canonical examples include the typical productivity rate of workers, or the average wage in a country. These quantities often have a few very high outliers that would distort the mean, so the median — which depends only on the middle position, not the specific values — gives a more honest summary.

CORE — when to prefer the MODE: When the question is 'what is the most frequent value?' or 'most popular item?', the mode is unambiguously the right choice. Examples include: the most-watched TV programme, the shoe size in greatest demand at a shoe shop, or the colour of vehicle used by most commuters.

KEY EMPIRICAL RELATION — 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean: For many real data sets, the three measures are related approximately by

  3 × Median ≈ Mode + 2 × Mean

This is called the empirical relationship among the three measures of central tendency. It is not an exact identity — it holds approximately for moderately skewed distributions — but it is useful for checking whether your computed values are mutually consistent, and for estimating a missing measure when the other two are known.

VERIFICATION (from earlier examples): Recall from M1.S2.T2 and M2.S4.T7 that for the 30-student marks distribution (Table 13.3):
  Mean = 62, Mode = 52.
Predicting the median via the empirical relation:
  3 × Median ≈ 52 + 2 × 62 = 52 + 124 = 176
  Median ≈ 176 / 3 ≈ 58.67

This is a reasonable estimate for the median of that data set — close to what a direct median computation would give (you can verify as an exercise using the cumulative frequency of Table 13.3).

WORKED EXAMPLE (decision-making, faded — you finish): A school principal wants to summarise this year's Class X board results for the parent newsletter. She has three questions:

  (a) How did the class as a whole perform compared to last year?
  (b) What was the typical score of a student?
  (c) Which score was most common among students?

For each question, identify which measure of central tendency is most appropriate and briefly justify why.

  (a) Use the MEAN, because it summarises the whole class and allows year-on-year comparison.
  (b) Use the MEDIAN (you complete the reasoning — think about why extreme performers should not skew the 'typical' value).
  (c) Use the MODE (you complete the reasoning — think about what 'most common' means precisely).

SUMMARY POINTS FROM THE CHAPTER:

1. The mean for grouped data can be found by three equivalent methods:
   • Direct Method: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ
   • Assumed Mean Method: x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ
   • Step-Deviation Method: x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h
   All three assume each class is centred at its mid-point (class mark).

2. The mode for grouped data is found by the modal-class interpolation formula:
   Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h

3. The cumulative frequency of a class is the sum of frequencies of all classes preceding it (plus the class itself for less-than-or-equal-to type).

4. The median for grouped data uses the median class and the formula:
   Median = l + ((n/2 − cf)/f) × h

A NOTE TO THE READER (from textbook): For calculating mode and median for grouped data, ensure that the class intervals are CONTINUOUS before applying the formulae. The same condition applies for construction of an ogive. Also, in ogives, the scale on the two axes may not be the same.

ERROR ALERT — 'one measure fits all': Students often pick whichever measure is easiest to compute rather than the one that answers the question. Stop and ask: 'what question am I really answering?' before picking a measure.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'mean, median, and mode should always agree': They often do not. The EXTENT of their disagreement measures the skewness of the data. Large gaps between mean and median indicate extreme values pulling the mean; a sharply different mode indicates clustering at a specific value.

topics.original_chunk:
Now, that you have studied about all the three measures of central tendency, let us discuss which measure would be best suited for a particular requirement.

The mean is the most frequently used measure of central tendency because it takes into account all the observations, and lies between the extremes, i.e., the largest and the smallest observations of the entire data. It also enables us to compare two or more distributions. For example, by comparing the average (mean) results of students of different schools of a particular examination, we can conclude which school has a better performance.

However, extreme values in the data affect the mean. For example, the mean of classes having frequencies more or less the same is a good representative of the data. But, if one class has frequency, say 2, and the five others have frequency 20, 25, 20, 21, 18, then the mean will certainly not reflect the way the data behaves. So, in such cases, the mean is not a good representative of the data.

In problems where individual observations are not important, and we wish to find out a 'typical' observation, the median is more appropriate, e.g., finding the typical productivity rate of workers, average wage in a country, etc. These are situations where extreme values may be there. So, rather than the mean, we take the median as a better measure of central tendency.

In situations which require establishing the most frequent value or most popular item, the mode is the best choice, e.g., to find the most popular T.V. programme being watched, the consumer item in greatest demand, the colour of the vehicle used by most of the people, etc.

Remarks:
1. There is a empirical relationship between the three measures of central tendency:
3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean
2. The median of grouped data with unequal class sizes can also be calculated. However, we shall not discuss it here.

Summary:
In this chapter, you have studied the following points:
1. The mean for grouped data can be found by:
   (i) the direct method: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ
   (ii) the assumed mean method: x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ
   (iii) the step deviation method: x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ) × h,
   with the assumption that the frequency of a class is centred at its mid-point, called its class mark.
2. The mode for grouped data can be found by using the formula:
   Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h
   where symbols have their usual meanings.
3. The cumulative frequency of a class is the frequency obtained by adding the frequencies of all the classes preceding the given class.
4. The median for grouped data is formed by using the formula:
   Median = l + ((n/2 − cf)/f) × h,
   where symbols have their usual meanings.

A Note to the Reader:
For calculating mode and median for grouped data, it should be ensured that the class intervals are continuous before applying the formulae. Same condition also apply for construction of an ogive. Further, in case of ogives, the scale may not be the same on both the axes.

Choose median when outliers skew the mean — for monthly wages of 10 workers where 1 earns ₹50,000 and the rest ₹8,000-₹12,000, the mean is pulled far above the typical wage; the median stays near the typical worker.
Choose mode when 'most popular' matters — to stock the most in-demand shoe size, the mode tells the shopkeeper which size to order the most.
Empirical cross-check — for the same distribution, if Mean = 62 and Mode = 52, predict: 3 × Median ≈ 52 + 2 × 62 = 176, so Median ≈ 58.7; verify this against a direct median calculation.

Additionally, the chapter introduces the empirical relation 3 × Median ≈ Mode + 2 × Mean, which holds for moderately skewed distributions and serves as a cross-check: for the 30-student distribution, Mean = 62 and Mode = 52 predict Median ≈ 58.67, consistent with a direct calculation.

topics.modified_chunk:
INTRODUCTION: This exercise set practises the median formula on seven real-world distributions, plus two 'mixed' questions that combine mean, median, and mode computations on the same data. Your workflow for each median question is: (1) build or read off the cumulative frequency column, (2) compute n/2 and locate the median class, (3) read off l, cf, f, h, (4) apply the formula.

STRATEGY GUIDE — for each question:

- Q1 (monthly electricity consumption, class size 20, n = 68): Asks for median, mean, AND mode. Build the cf column first: 4, 9, 22, 42, 56, 64, 68. n/2 = 34, so median class is 125-145 (cf = 42 first crosses 34). For mean, Step-Deviation with a = 135, h = 20 is most efficient. For mode, modal class is 125-145 (frequency 20). Compare all three and note whether the empirical relation 3M ≈ Mo + 2Mean holds approximately.

- Q2 (missing frequencies x, y, median = 28.5, n = 60): Reverse problem analogous to Example 8. Median class is 20-30 (median 28.5 lies in it). Write cf symbolically: 5, 5+x, 25+x, 40+x, 40+x+y, 45+x+y. Total = 45+x+y = 60 gives x + y = 15. Apply formula to get a second equation. Solve the 2×2 system.

- Q3 (ages of policy holders, cumulative less-than form): Given as 'Below 20: 2, Below 25: 6, Below 30: 24, ...'. But the first class STARTS at 18 (not 0), since policies are only for ages 18 and above. Convert to per-class frequencies: 18-20 has 2, 20-25 has 4, 25-30 has 18, etc. Total n = 100, so n/2 = 50. Median class = 35-40 (cf first crosses 50).

- Q4 (leaf lengths, DISCRETE classes 118-126, 127-135, ...): Must convert to continuous: 117.5-126.5, 126.5-135.5, ..., 171.5-180.5 (the hint in the textbook says this explicitly). Only after conversion apply the median formula.

- Q5 (lamp lifetimes, class size 500): Direct application. cf column: 14, 70, 130, 216, 290, 352, 400. n/2 = 200. Median class is 3000-3500 (cf = 216 first crosses 200).

- Q6 (surname letters, mixed): Asks for median, mean, AND mode. Note that classes 1-4, 4-7 are already continuous (the upper limit of one equals the lower limit of the next). Median class and modal class coincide at 7-10 (frequency 40, and cf at 7-10 first crosses n/2 = 50). Mean via Direct Method with class marks 2.5, 5.5, 8.5, 11.5, 14.5, 17.5.

- Q7 (weights of 30 students, class size 5): cf: 2, 5, 13, 19, 25, 28, 30. n/2 = 15. Median class = 55-60 (cf = 19 first crosses 15).

WORKED STRATEGY DEMO (Q1, complete): Monthly electricity consumption of 68 consumers.

| Monthly consumption (in units) | Number of consumers (f) | cf |
| 65-85 | 4 | 4 |
| 85-105 | 5 | 9 |
| 105-125 | 13 | 22 |
| 125-145 | 20 | 42 |
| 145-165 | 14 | 56 |
| 165-185 | 8 | 64 |
| 185-205 | 4 | 68 |

MEDIAN: n = 68, n/2 = 34. Median class = 125-145 (cf = 42 first crosses 34). l = 125, cf (preceding) = 22, f = 20, h = 20.

  Median = 125 + ((34 − 22)/20) × 20 = 125 + 12 = 137 units.

MEAN: Class marks 75, 95, 115, 135, 155, 175, 195. Pick a = 135, h = 20. Then uᵢ = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. fᵢuᵢ = −12, −10, −13, 0, 14, 16, 12. Σfᵢuᵢ = 7. Σfᵢ = 68.

  Mean = 135 + 20 × (7/68) = 135 + 2.06 = 137.06 units (approximately).

MODE: Modal class 125-145 (max frequency 20). l = 125, h = 20, f₁ = 20, f₀ = 13, f₂ = 14.

  Mode = 125 + ((20 − 13) / (40 − 13 − 14)) × 20 = 125 + (7/13) × 20 = 125 + 10.77 = 135.77 units.

COMPARISON: All three measures fall close together in the range 135-137 units, signalling that the distribution is roughly symmetric. Check the empirical relation: 3 × 137 = 411; Mode + 2 × Mean = 135.77 + 274.12 = 409.89. The two sides differ by only about 1 unit — the relation holds well.

PARTIALLY FADED DEMO (Q2, you complete): Median = 28.5, n = 60.

Step 1: cf column in terms of x, y: 5, 5+x, 25+x, 40+x, 40+x+y, 45+x+y.
Step 2: 45 + x + y = 60 ⇒ x + y = 15.  ...(1)
Step 3: Median 28.5 lies in class 20-30. So median class = 20-30. l = 20, f = 20, cf (preceding) = 5 + x, h = 10.
Step 4: Apply median formula.

  28.5 = 20 + ((30 − (5 + x))/20) × 10

You finish: solve for x, then use equation (1) to find y. (Expected answer: x = 8, y = 7.)

ERROR ALERT — common pitfalls in this exercise:
1. Not converting discrete classes (like 118-126 in Q4) to continuous before applying the median formula.
2. Using the cf of the median class itself (instead of the preceding class) in the formula.
3. In cumulative less-than problems (Q3, Q7-style), forgetting that the 'Below 20' row represents the class interval starting wherever the data legitimately starts (here 18-20), not 0-20.
4. For missing-frequency problems, forgetting that the total-frequency equation is only ONE condition; the second condition comes from the median formula itself.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK — 'median and mean always fall in the same class': They can fall in different classes. In Q1 above they happened to coincide in 125-145, but this is not guaranteed.

CHECK-IN before you begin: For each problem, first write the cf column completely. If the cf doesn't end at n, you have an arithmetic error; fix it before trying the median formula.

Empirical relation: 3 × Median ≈ Mode + 2 × Mean.
3 × Median ≈ 135.8 + 2 × 137.1 = 135.8 + 274.2 = 410.
Estimated Median ≈ 410 / 3 ≈ 136.7.

Direct median calculation (for verification): n/2 = 33.5; cumulative frequencies: 4, 9, 22, 42 → median class = 125-145. l = 125, cf = 22, f = 20, h = 20.
Median = 125 + ((33.5−22)/20) × 20 = 125 + 11.5 = 136.5.

Comparison: Mean ≈ 137.1, Median ≈ 136.5, Mode ≈ 135.8. All three are very close, confirming the distribution is nearly symmetric. The empirical estimate (136.7) is within 0.2 of the direct value (136.5) — confirming the relation holds well for this distribution.

recall_questions.answer: Report the mean when comparing distributions or summarising overall performance — for example, to decide which of two Mumbai schools performed better in a board exam, compare their mean marks, since the mean uses all observations equally. Report the median when the data has extreme outliers or skewness — for example, to describe the typical monthly income of auto-rickshaw drivers in Chennai, the median is more honest than the mean (which would be pulled up by a few high-earners). Report the mode when the question is about the most popular or most common value — for example, to decide which kurta size to stock most at a Diwali sale in a Delhi store, the modal size is the direct answer.
recall_questions.prompt: Summarise in three sentences: when should a researcher report the mean, when the median, and when the mode for grouped data? Use one concrete Indian-context example for each.

modules.detailed_summary: Module 3 completes the chapter's central toolkit by adding the median to the mean and mode already studied. The module opens with a recap of the ungrouped median from Class IX, then builds cumulative frequency distributions of both the less-than and more-than-or-equal-to types. These tables allow the student to locate the median class — the interval that brackets the n/2 th observation — and then apply the linear interpolation formula Median = l + ((n/2 − cf)/f) × h to pinpoint the median within that class. Two worked examples illustrate the formula directly, including a harder case where the median is given and missing frequencies must be found by combining the formula with the total-frequency condition. A culminating REVIEW topic shows when to prefer mean, median, or mode, and derives the empirical relation 3 × Median ≈ Mode + 2 × Mean. The module closes with Exercise 13.3 mixed practice, which asks for all three measures from a single distribution and their comparison.
important_points: the median is a measure of central tendency which gives the value of the middle-most observation in the data.
if n is odd, the median is the ((n+1)/2)th observation. And, if n is even, then the median will be the average of the (n/2)th and the ((n/2)+1)th observations.
the cumulative frequency of a class is the frequency obtained by adding frequencies of all the classes preceding the given class.
